1.	Is the CBC changing its commercial advertising policy with four rather than three minutes of commercial time per half-hour on television now being available?
2.	If so, what are the reasons for this change in policy?

November 17, 1969
Questions

I am informed by the CBC as follows: 1. Prior to the present programming year, the allowable commercial content for all sponsored programs on the French Television Network and English Metro-Net (CBC-owned stations) and for selectively sponsored programs on both English and French CBC-owned television stations was four minutes per half-hour. Full English network sponsors were limited to three minutes plus billboards after 6:00 p.m. With the beginning of the 1969/70 program season the "four-minute format" was extended to all sponsored half-hour programs on the full English Television Network, as has been the case on the French TV Network.
2.	The increase in allowable commercial content on the full English network not only brings all phases of the Corporation's commercial operations into line but it also puts the CBC in step with all private segments of the television industry in Canada, both on a network and selective basis. Since the four-minute format is now the rule, rather than the exception, Canadian advertisers have oriented their sales and marketing strategy accordingly. The extra minute results in both the major and minor sponsor on alternate weeks receiving an equal amount of advertising time in each program, i.e., two minutes for each half hour of programming. This provides the kind of continuous program identification that advertisers have come to expect from alternate week sponsorship.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 EXTERNAL AFFAIRS BIAFRA-AID FOR STARVING-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 EXTERNAL AFFAIRS BIAFRA-AID FOR STARVING-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 26 I move, seconded by the hon. member for Greenwood, the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the Prime Minister's answer to a question on Friday, reported at page 824 of Hansard, stating that the Biafran authorities do not permit daylight flights and are using night flights of relief supplies in order to screen shipments of arms. I might say that the concluding words have been changed from the words actually used by the Prime Minister, which were "bring in shipments of arms".
In view of the fact that this statement may seriously prejudice the longstanding Canadian tradition of neutrality, as well as endanger the extensive relief operation upon which the lives of millions of civilians depend, I ask Your Honour to give consideration to allowing this motion to be put.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 EXTERNAL AFFAIRS BIAFRA-AID FOR STARVING-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
The hon. member for Fundy-Royal has proposed to move the adjournment of the House under the provisions of Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a statement made by the Prime Minister on Friday last. As the hon. member for Fundy-Royal knows, and as all hon. members know, what the Chair has to determine is not whether the matter itself is one of importance but whether the House should be adjourned for an emergency debate under the terms of Standing Order 26.
The Standing Order cannot be invoked to initiate a debate about an issue which is of a continuing nature. It would appear that even when one takes into full account the observation by the Prime Minister to which the hon. member alluded, the essence of the problem is one which hon. members have had in mind for many months and, indeed, have debated 21362-561
Inquiries of the Ministry in this House on several occasions. Even if it were argued that a new dimension has been added, the substance of the matter remains the same and, unfortunately, is likely to remain the same for a while yet.
The Standing Order also requires the Chair to pay regard to the probability of the matter being brought before the House within a reasonable time by other means. I should think there will be a number of such opportunities. For these reasons I must rule, with some regrets, that the hon. member's proposed motion cannot be submitted to the House at this time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: NIGERIA-BIAFRA-POSITION ON CIVIL WAR, RELIEF AND ARMS SHIPMENTS
speechtext: My question is directed to the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker. It concerns the right hon. gentleman's comment on Friday accusing the Biafran authorities of using relief agencies to bring in arms shipments, or to screen arms shipments. Can the Prime Minister tell the House whether this extremely partisan denunciation of Colonel Ojukwu indicates that Canada has abandoned its posture of non-involvement or neutrality in connection with the civil war and that the government is now committed to full support of the position of General Gowon and the federal Nigerian authorities?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: NIGERIA-BIAFRA-POSITION ON CIVIL WAR, RELIEF AND ARMS SHIPMENTS
speechtext:
We have always taken the position, Mr. Speaker, that General Gowon headed the legitimate government in Nigeria and that Colonel Ojukwu was the leader of a secessionist group. The Canadian government has always managed to stay out of this civil war despite the proddings of both opposition parties to become involved, through the use of our aircraft and so on, on the secessionist side. Our position has not changed, but as observers of this civil war we feel that we have reached the stage at which it is obvious to this government and, perhaps, to more Canadians than previously, that Colonel Ojukwu is really not interested in allowing daylight flights.
The suggestion regarding daylight flights has been put to him in a variety of ways by this government, by the United States govern-

November 17, 1969
Inquiries of the Ministry ment and by other governments, not directly but by making available to him ways in which the Red Cross could commence daylight flights. Colonel Ojukwu has never seen his way clear to receive such flights, and that is why we regretfully draw the conclusion that Colonel Ojukwu is less concerned with starving children in Biafra than he is with receiving arms and perhaps scoring political propaganda victories across the world.

subsubtopic: NIGERIA-BIAFRA-POSITION ON CIVIL WAR, RELIEF AND ARMS SHIPMENTS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister stated that the Biafran authorities are using night flights for the purpose of bringing in arms. I should like to know whether this statement is based on surmise or upon information provided by relief agencies working in the area. Would the Prime Minister indicate from where he gets his information, in view of the fact that our observer teams seem only to have visited that part of Nigeria controlled by the federal authorities. Would the Prime Minister indicate on what source of information he bases these very serious charges?

subsubtopic: NIGERIA-BIAFRA-POSITION ON CIVIL WAR, RELIEF AND ARMS SHIPMENTS
speechtext:
The source is Colonel
Ojukwu himself and the Biafran authorities, who seem to be intent on cooking up reasons for not accepting daylight flights. The I.C.R.C.-the International Committee of the Red Cross-the Canadian Red Cross, the Canadian government, the United States government and other governments, have been proposing ways in which supplies of food, drugs and other medicines can be brought into Biafra if only the Biafran authorities would allow the airstrip to be used during daytime.
The I.C.R.C. have been negotiating with the Nigerian authorities an agreement whereby the forces of Nigeria would let daylight flights take place for the purpose of bringing in relief supplies. The Canadian government has discussed the possibility of supplying observers on the I.C.R.C. flights to make sure that these flights bring in food and medical supplies only, thereby guaranteeing to the Nigerians that the daylight flights would not be used to bring in arms. Always, for one reason or another, the Biafran authorities have refused these daylight flights. I suggest that if the members of the opposition and other people in this country who are sympathetic to the plight of the Biafran civilian population would only look at the situation objectively they might cease swallowing Biafran propaganda and make it easier for the I.C.R.C. to bring in daylight flights with relief supplies.
IMr. Trudeau.I

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I put this question to the Prime Minister. subsubtopic: NIGERIA-BIAFRA-POSITION ON CIVIL WAR, RELIEF AND ARMS SHIPMENTS
speechtext: Not at all, Mr. Speaker. We are prepared to consider other ways of getting supplies to the starving people of Biafra. We have suggested other ways, including airdrops, use of helicopters, river crossings and so on. It always happens that the Biafran authorities do not see their way clear to accepting these alternative ways. As I said the other day, the question is not the availability of supplies. It is not as though there is nothing available to send in the way of food and other supplies to Biafra. It is the way of getting them in which poses the problem. The hon. member should not draw the conclusion that we are not interested in making supplies available. We have not yet come up with any more sensible way of doing this than by bringing supplies in by day, and I am surprised that the opposition does not support us on this.

subsubtopic: NIGERIA-BIAFRA-POSITION ON CIVIL WAR, RELIEF AND ARMS SHIPMENTS
speechtext: Will the government not consider using the available means now being used, namely, Canairelief and joint churchaid which are actually doing the job now but need the help of this government?

I repeat that the easiest way of doing so would be to permit daylight flights, and we can see no sensible argument beyond the propaganda one for refusing such daylight flights.

other than the hon. member who spoke the words? If the Prime Minister himself did not make the change, I believe it should not have been made by anyone on his behalf. In addition to Dean Cohen the following persons comprised the committee: Dr. J. A. Corry, Principal, Queens University; l'abbe Gerard Dion, Faculty of Social Sciences, Laval University; Mr. Saul Hayes, Q.C., Executive Vice-President, Canadian Jewish Congress; Professor Mark R. Following the committee's report in November, 1965, the bill was introduced as Bill S-49. This was during the 27th parliament, 1966-67. On November 7, that bill was given first reading and on March 20 it was read a second time on division in the other place and referred to a special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons for consideration. In the second session of the 27th parliament the provisions of Bill S-49 were introduced as Bill S-5. That bill also received first and second reading and on November 21, 1967 and was referred to a special committee of the Senate, which had already been appointed on November 2, 1967. The special committee of the Senate met and heard evidence on three occasions early in 1968. I believe the dates were February 14 and 29 and March 7. However, the 27th parliament came to an end on April 23, before the bill could be further considered.
The bill was again introduced in the same form as previous bills in the first session of the 28th parliament, as Bill S-21, was again given first and second readings and referred to the Senate Standing Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs. The standing committee held 11 public meetings, heard 32 witnesses and received representations from some 17 organizations. The Senate committee presented its report, which was adopted on June 17, 1969, and on the same day the Senate read the bill a third time on division and passed it. It should perhaps be mentioned here that Bill S-21, as passed by the Senate, was amended in certain respects. By way of general comment only, and without getting into the details of the bill, by way of a trespass upon the rules of this House, the offence of advocating genocide was modified so as to include two acts and not five. In addition, that offence was made referable to an "identifiable group" which is to be tested or determined by reference to "religion" as well as by the other tests of colour, race or ethnic origin. The definition of an identifiable group was changed by the addition of the term "religion". In addition, a new definition was added to safeguard freedom of expression on a religious subject and this addition was tied in with the addition of "religion" as one of the tests of an identifiable group. The requirement of the consent of the Attorney General was added in relation to the offences of advocating or promoting genocide, of wilful promotion of hatred and contempt and also in relation to the in rem forfeiture provisions. I pointed out that the present Bill C-3 is in exactly the same form as Bill S-21 which received first reading in the House of Commons last June 19, as I previously mentioned.

At this point I would like to summarize briefly the main effects of this bill. If the biff is enacted by parliament, it will create three new offences: First, the offence of advocating or promoting genocide; second, the offence of public incitement of hatred and contempt likely to lead to a breach of the peace; third, wilful promotion of hatred or contempt. In addition, the bill provides for in rem proceedings that will permit the seizure and forfeiture of hate propaganda publications.
The bill defines genocide so as to include two specific acts, namely the killing of members of any identifiable group or the deliberate inflicting of conditions of life calculated to bring about the physical destruction of an identifiable group. The offences of public incitement, of hatred and contempt and wilful promotion of hatred and contempt are constituted by "communicating statements." "Communicating statements" is broadly defined so as to include all forms of audible or visual communication.
The consent of the Attorneys-General of the provinces will be required for prosecution of the offences of advocating genocide and wilful promotion of hatred. It will also be required for the institution of the in rem proceedings. However, prosecution of the public incitement offence, that is to say public incitement of hatred and contempt likely to lead to a breach of the public order or peace, does not require the consent of the Attorney-General. Obviously, if the probable effect would be calculated to involve the public order, then the reason for requiring the consent of the Attorney-General would not be as pertinent since the essence of the offence is the likelihood of a breach of the peace.
While no statutory defence is provided in the case of the public incitement offence, in the case of the wilful promotion offence, three statutory defences are provided. The first is related to the expression of opinion on a religious subject. The second and third can be regarded as the standard defamatory libel defences of truth or, alternatively, reasonable belief in the truth of the statement combined with public interest in the statement.
I am of course fully aware of the significant objections that have been taken against this bill by a number of very prominent persons who are as vitally concerned as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and I are with the problem of civil rights. Some of these persons have said that the bill is not necessary and that the criminal law process should not be used for this purpose. In the alternative, they say that the provisions of the Criminal Code

are sufficient to deal with the problems as they now stand.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HATE PROPAGANDA
speechtext:
Thank you.
I may say at the outset that we support the principle of the bill. I do not think there will be any argument from our side as far as the first part of the bill is concerned, that is to say, the part which states that anyone who advocates or promotes genocide is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for five years. Nevertheless, some questions arise with reference to the concluding clauses, and this is why their provisions will have to be studied with extreme care.
The rationale behind this bill, it seems to us, is that on the balance of public convenience and inconvenience the state should use the criminal law to curtail the right of freedom of speech and the right to privacy in order to prevent the defamation of identifiable groups on the grounds that such defamation might:
1. intimidate or cause mental anguish to a member of such a group; 2. foster a public opinion which, in a suitable combination of sociological, economic and political circumstances, might enable a State to commit genocide against such a group; and
3.	in a particular instance, be likely to cause a disturbance in a public place either by inciting violence against a group or violence by the group against the defamer.
I think we need to look at history in order to understand the background of this legislation. In our own generation, in our own lifetime, we have witnessed what is probably the most brutal, barbaric and inhuman treatment of a certain race, of people belonging to a certain religion, in the course of which they were virtually wiped out in several states in Europe. With this in mind, one is bound to support those provisions of the bill which deal with the subject of genocide.
Until the establishment of the United Nations, civil libertarians concentrated their efforts on attaining and enshrining the fundamental freedoms of speech, press, religion, assembly and association. Since then, and to a large extent because of the influence through the United Nations of the newly independent countries of Africa and Asia, increasing emphasis has been placed on the establishment of the right of everyone to equal treatment, regardless of race, religion, colour, sex, national or ethnic origin.
Here in Canada, I feel, we can take some pride in having to a large extent achieved these aims. This emphasis on the right to equal treatment has been asserted not only against governments and public institutions,

November 17, 1969
Criminal Code
but also against private individuals and organizations. The focus has been on removing the overt acts of discrimination such as the denial of civic and economic equality, and the denial of equal access to employment and accommodation. However, more recently it has been asserted that one of the major lessons we should have learned from the Hitler era was that the ideal of an egalitarian society may be impossible to achieve when the dissemination of racist ideas is permitted. The promotion of hatred against identifiable groups in our society, even if the number of hate propagandists is small, constitutes a danger to a modern democratic society. There has been advocacy of restricting such vilification, even if this is achieved only by restricting certain basic rights of expression.
I do not think there is anything in the Code which directly covers the first part of the bill, though, of course, once an overt act takes place, committed by any person or group of persons, it would, under the Code, constitute murder. Let me draw attention to section 166, which deals with the spreading of false news. This is to be found in Crankshaw's 1959 edition-the latest edition-at page 227. We read:
Every one who wilfully publishes a statement, tale or news that he knows is false and that causes or is likely to cause injury or mischief to a public interest is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years.
This is the old offence under common law, prosecutions for which seem to have fallen out of fashion. In 1778 there was a case of this kind in which the defendant was indicted for having unlawfully, wickedly and maliciously published false news whereby discord might grow between the King and his subjects or the great men of the realm, by publishing and placarding a printed paper or notice falsely announcing that an order-incouncil had been made by the King proclaiming war with France. This is an old case, referred to as Scott's case; it is to be found in the New Newgate Calendar. It has been decided in Canada that publication of a placard stating that settlers from the United States are not wanted in Canada is an injury to the public interest and that the person wilfully and knowingly publishing such false statements was guilty of spreading false news. This is the case of R. v. Hoaglin. It has further been held that an accused who has been acquitted on a charge of publishing a seditious libel cannot afterward be prosecuted in respect of the same publication of spreading false news and that the words "whereby

injury or mischief is occasioned to any public interest" in the latter section must contemplate a seditious intention, since the section is included under the general heading "Seditious Offences".
a (3.20 p.m.)
So, the subject is at least partially covered by the Code at the present time. One of the complaints which has been received is that the bill does not really follow the Cohen report. The minister himself told us that when the measure was before the Senate many people attacked it because in their view it would destroy the greatest civil right enjoyed by any democracy, namely, freedom of speech. This is something at which the committee must take a serious look.
As I pointed out at the beginning, I want to make it very clear that we agree with the principle contained in the first part of the bill without any reservation whatever, particularly in view of what happened in Europe during our generation.
However, I should like to quote from an article in the Globe and Mail that deals with a matter that the committee must approach with great care and study. This article deals with a position that was taken by many witnesses who appeared before the Senate committee, people from across Canada who had distinguished themselves not only as lawyers but in the field of sociology and other fields. This article reads in part:
There is every indication that a Canadian hate bill would have the same effect.
That is a reference to what happened in Great Britain, where the legislation, instead of helping the people it was intended to serve, worked against them.
It could become one of the most iniquitous and oppressive pieces of legislation in the books. There are several volatile issues in Canada. Language is one: religious differences between Protestants and Catholics constitute another. Walk into an urban renewal area in almost any city and you'll find residents who are trigger-tense. The greatest potential the bill has is for backfiring.
In other words, the bill may work against the group that we are trying to protect.
The ludicrous aspect of the hate bill is that the laws of criminal libel provide the same protection against dissemination of hate while, at the same time, offering safeguards to freedom of speech and guarantees against unjust prosecution that the hate bill doesn't have.
Too often the bill is characterized by its supporters as legislating against the virulent kind of hate that leads to genocide. That is a false picture. The bill contains a section making it a crime to advocate or promote genocide.
November 17, 1969

That is on all fours with what I say about the principle of this bill.
The remaining sections deal with inciting or promoting hatred or contempt of any group that can be identified by race, colour, religion or ethnic origin.
If I may just pause there. As the minister knows, the bill that was before the Senate made no provisions regarding religious groups, but this has been remedied by the new bill. I think this change resulted from the evidence given by the witnesses who appeared before the Senate committee, particularly by the Very Reverend Ernest Marshall Howse of the United Church. The Globe and Mail article continues:
There's a world of difference between promoting contempt and advocating genocide.
The widespread concern expressed during the three years that the bill has been contemplated should demand second thoughts from members of parliament, now that the bill has been introduced in the House.
These second thoughts are going to be shared by the committee. Let me tell the minister that we have a good standing committee. We work well together. Members of all parties generally agree with most amendments that are made to the Criminal Code. I hope that in this case the committee will be able to hear evidence, as did the Senators, regarding incitement of hate and contempt with which the second part of the bill deals.
At this point, may I bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, a matter of concern to those on this side of the House. I refer to a particular philosophy that is becoming increasingly evident on the part of the government. In fact, the minister himself touched on this matter when he addressed the Canadian Bar Association and talked about placing control over wire tapping in the hands of the Attorney General of Canada and the Attorneys General of the various provinces.
According to the amendment contained in clause 1, no proceeding for an offence under Section 267a shall be instituted without the consent of the Attorney General. That is a proceeding connected with genocide. The same provision is made in the proposed section 267b which deals with public incitement of hatred.
My fear about this provision is this. Take the case of a group of persons who are charged under this section because the Attorney General of Canada or the Attorney General of a province thinks they are committing genocide or inciting hatred. Another group of persons may act in identical fashion, but the
Criminal Code
Attorney General, in his own good graces, for political or other reasons, does not feel they are inciting hatred or committing genocide, and thus no charges are laid.
This is a situation that could occur and I submit that these provisions establish a very dangerous precedent. If these provisions are accepted, then the Attorney General of Canada and the Attorneys General of the provinces are given too much power. After all, such appointments are made by the Prime Minister of Canada and the Premiers of the provinces. Basically, these appointees are responsible within their own jurisdictions for the administration of justice in Canada. Nevertheless, they are elected by political parties, and to that extent are partisan. They are appointed by cabinets and are political animals. They are appointed by governments to administer justice as well as they can. I also suggest that far too much power is given the Minister of Justice and the Attorneys General of the various provinces in the matter of freedom of speech, which is one of the great civil liberties of any democracy.
We are all aware of the fact that the present Minister of Justice will not always be minister, and I do not question his integrity here. But I repeat that certain groups may be charged under the first part of the bill or under the second part simply because the Attorney General of Canada or the Attorneys General of the provinces feel a charge should be laid, whereas another group performing identical acts may be let off the hook. This is one of the first problems, as far as I can see, with which the committee will have to come to grips when it begins study of the bill.

The Cohen committee stressed that the definition of genocide should be restricted to "the annihilation of identifiable groups for no other reason than they are what they are". The committee did not want to include advocacy and promotion of revolution against constituted authority because it was prepared to concede "as a philosophical argument that there may be a genuine social interest in not totally excluding advocacy and promotion of violence against state authorities-"

Of course, we see today that the protest movement has grown as never before, and States are now accepting open protests. There is no doubt about the fact that democracy is working in the streets. That is why there has been some criticism of the right to freedom of speech, to speak one's mind. There has been some criticism of what is taking place today in a city in Canada. There have been similar protests to those that took place in the United States and, whether or not you agree with those who are protesting they were quiet, orderly and peaceful. This right to protest

constitutes one form of freedom of speech. Of course, freedom of speech means not only the right to speak, but also the right to be silent. That, in itself, is freedom of speech.
Let me once again emphasize that we are in favour of the first part of the bill. We are in favour of the principle of the bill because the principle is that, on a balance of public convenience and inconvenience, the State should use the criminal law to curtail the right to freedom of speech and the right to privacy in order to prevent the crime of genocide. We are on all fours in that respect.
We must examine very carefully the second part of the bill, because in a democratic State one of the most important civil liberties is the right to freedom of speech. The Globe and Mail states that the ludicrous aspect of the hate bill is that the laws of criminal libel provide the same protection. I should like to hear witnesses appearing before the committee set out fully the law with regard to that particular subject as it now exists in the Criminal Code. I am sure the members of this party want to be assured that this Provision is not a duplication or an extension of a Provision which is already contained in the law. If it is an extension, I should like to know that it is not really taking away freedom of speech, particularly in a democratic State such as we have.
I also hope that the committee members will study very carefully the submissions made by all the witnesses at the Senate hearings so there will be no duplication. We should have a look at what Professor Scott had to say as reported at page 202 of the proceedings of the Senate Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs, number 9. He was called as a witness and dealt with this particular aspect of freedom of speech as related to these sections. He said:
There are two positions. We had crisis legislation in 1919 following the Winnipeg strike, which was a crisis. In the other case, the "Padlock Act", there was no crisis at all; just general legislation against propagating Communism, in 1938.
Then we come to that great legal decade of the fifties when the Supreme Court of Canada enlarged the concept of human rights in a series of magnificent cases, of which this country should be proud. I will mention only a few. There was the Boucher case, which defined the law of sedition and eliminated precisely the factor this bill would re-introduce. That is why I say that this bill is retrograde. The law has advanced and this will take it back.
Then, there was a question asked by Senator Phillips who said:
Would you develop that a little more, Professor Scott, for a few moments?
November 17, 1969

Then, Professor Scott stated:
The old law, sedition, counted as an element in sedition the raising of ill-will between different classes of His Majesty's subjects, and dividing one class from another. This could be dividing a race from another. That used to be sufficient, in itself, to constitute sedition. The Supreme Court in the Boucher case said it was not sufficient in itself to constitute the crime of sedition unless it was accompanied with words or provocations or incitements which were likely to lead to a breach of the peace.
So, basically when the Supreme Court interpreted the law on sedition, it actually covered most of what is contained in this bill. Professor Scott went on to state:
In other words, under the Boucher decision we were told in Canada that we could publish or utter statements that might have an incidental effect of making people angry and causing a certain amount of ill-will, but it was not illegal until it reached that point where the peace was threatened.
This is like civil law where there has to be a trespass before you can start an action. You just cannot say there will be a trespass, there actually has to be an overt act. The same rule applies here; the peace must be threatened or there must be a reasonable belief that the peace is threatened.
If this bill passes the state of the law will be back to what it was before the Boucher case. I will never forget how delighted all my friends were when the Supreme Court came out with what we thought was a clarification of the law regarding freedom of speech, yet still provided us in Canada with adequate protection against the real danger. In other words, Professor Scott is saying, that a retrograde step was actually taken in respect of those people who dared to stand up to management in 1919. He suggests it would be a backward step if we were to return to the Padlock Law. There must be some over act, as a result of which the peace is threatened.
Let me come back to the peaceful protests that took place in Canada. This is a form of action taken to express an opinion. One need not agree with the people in universities or the people in the streets who protest, but providing the protest is peaceful and the aim of those who protest is not to damage property or to run slipshod over the civil rights of other people, then such protests fall within the right to freedom of speech. This is a right of the people to express themselves, as the people in the United States recently expressed their opinion against the war in Viet Nam. The recent protest march in Washington was one of the largest, but it was quiet and peaceful.

The people in Canada and other democracies must have the right to this kind of protest and must have the right to freedom of speech. If you take away this right you are setting the law back several years, in fact to the last century. As the Globe and Mail suggested, we can go along with the first part of the bill, but the second part might erode or take away freedom of speech not only in respect of our newspapers, radio and television, but in respect of those who assemble in our streets to protest.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this party or most of its members at least, will support this bill. We propose to suggest modifications which we hope will be given full consideration by the committee and will be considered by the minister even before we reach the committee stage. I will outline later on the modifications I propose.
In my view, this bill is directed toward a real, a very great and palpable evil, the evil of deliberate and wilful dissemination of racial hatred. In my view it is the duty of parliament, now that it has the opportunity, to declare that the purposeful incitement of hatred of racial groups is contrary to the moral sense of the Canadian community and ought to be prescribed by law. I am fully aware, as other speakers have said, that there are many staunch defenders of civil liberties who are uneasy about this legislation. My view, on balance, is that this legislation merely prescribes the reasonable limit, by any fair and sensible interpretation, of the ordinary freedom of speech and freedom of expression. There is a real problem. The problem that faces the legislature in dealing with hate propaganda is how to balance freedom of expression on the one hand against abuse by incitement of hatred and violence on the other. There are admittedly two contrary views. The first stresses the danger to freedom of critical expression which we all admit and proclaim is fundamental to our whole system.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
It is said that this danger is inherent in any attempt to prohibit or penalize controversial or even offensive modes of speech or writing. According to this school of thought, the disseminators of hate propaganda are only of trifling influence. It is said that unbalanced individuals are more likely to be encouraged by martyrdom, suppression and the attendant publicity, than they are to be deterred. They simply do not deserve to be or are not worthy

November 17, 1969
Criminal Code
to be noticed by the law. It is argued that the dangers of hate propaganda are minimal in Canada. It is said the attitudes of mind revealed by such publications and those likely to be affected by them should be dealt with by education and not by legislation. Legislation, it is argued, cannot be adequately and precisely framed in such a way as not to infringe on legitimate freedom of expression.
I want to put forward the other side of the argument which stresses the grave consequences revealed by history of racial hatred in a world compelled by technology to become a "neighbourhood". This side of the argument emphasizes the historic and necessary recognition of limitations to such concepts as freedom of speech which no more than any other concept or freedom can be interpreted as an absolute. It is said there is a widespread but generally latent tendency to hostility toward other groups which can be, and is, exploited by systematic and sometimes skilful promotion of hatred. It is argued on this side-and I accept this argument-that there is an important educative effect in positive legal pronouncements and sanctions and it is an error to keep legislation and education as mutually exclusive alternatives. Both are necessary to deal with this evil.
It is my view that there is need for remedial legislation and that this legislation does not in fact impinge upon any reasonable interpretation of freedom of speech. I do accept the broadest definition of freedom of speech. Indeed, I should like to quote to this House the words of Mr. Justice Rand in the Boucher case already referred to by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). In that case, Mr. Justice Rand said:
Freedom in thought and speech and disagreement in ideas and beliefs, on every conceivable subject, are of the essence of our life. The clash of critical discussion on political, social and religious subjects has too deeply become the stuff of daily experience to suggest that mere ill-will as a product can strike down the latter with illegality.
If it were not disrespectful I would say to Mr. Justice Rand, "Hear, hear". I subscribe to that. What is involved in this legislation is the deliberate fomenting of hatred on the basis of races, groups and religions. That I suggest is quite a different thing from merely ill will. Some people are very exercised about infringement on freedom of speech. Surely, they must recognize that from time immemorial there have been necessary limitations upon freedom of speech. Our laws of libel and slander are the clearest exposition of that. They apply to private individuals. It is
[Mr. Brewln.j
recognized that I have no right to destroy my neighbour's reputation by repeating falsehoods about him. By what reasoning then can it be said that the destruction of the reputation and good name of a group of people should not also be condemned. This is just as dangerous in its implication and just as harmful and painful to the victims or recipients as individual defamation. But this for some reason or other is said to be sacrosanct and should be preserved in the name of freedom of speech.
I suggest that our ready and proper acceptance of limitations in respect of the laws of libel apply to group libel as much as private libel. It is said that some of us, including myself, in this party have suggested that the recently passed by-law in Montreal should be submitted to the courts and that we are opposed to its as an infringement of civil liberties. The question then is asked, is it consistent with that view to come forward in this House now and support this bill? I say there is all the difference in the world between these things. In our view, the Montreal by-law is clearly criminal law which is exclusively within the powers of parliament. It is our view that the Montreal by-law clearly infringes upon the legitimate and traditional exercise of the right of demonstration and free speech which has been said by the courts to be the breath of life of parliamentary institutions. But the legislation we are discussing can hardly be said to be other than criminal law and, therefore, its constitutionality cannot be questioned.
There is no parliamentary right to defame and incite hatred against whole groups of people. The Montreal legislation is clearly unnecessary because there is already adequate legislation. I agree with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) that the same cannot be said in this particular field. The question may be asked, why should we bother with legislation unless there is a real threat. I should like to read one paragraph or two from the report on hate propaganda prepared, as the minister told us, by Professor Cohen with some distinguished colleagues including the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. Mac-Guigan). I should like to read from page 12 of that report which tells about what is happening in Canada, not somewhere else:
The current hate campaign dates from early 1963, when it began in the Toronto area. Since then it has extended to several other centres in Ontario, and to at least seven other provinces: British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Quebec; but the main
November 17, 1969

activities have been essentially in Ontario and to a lesser extent in Quebec and in British Columbia. From 1963 on there was and continues to be a steady dissemination of hate propaganda, mainly antiJewish, anti-Negro and neo-Nazi in nature. The propaganda has been plastered and displayed in conspicuous places, distributed at public gatherings, placed in apartment mailboxes, sent through the regular mails, and scattered from the upper floors of downtown buildings to the streets below.
The printed, mimeographed and other written materials seem to be obtained in large measure, although not exclusively, from American sources. In many instances it is mailed directly from Arlington, Virginia, the headquarters of the American Nazi Party and the World Union of National Socialists, and from Birmingham, Alabama-[DOT]
And so on. So, there cannot be any doubt that this country has witnessed a sustained campaign to disseminate hate literature. I shall not go into the details of this, but I believe that anyone who intends to speak on this subject should take the trouble to read some of the literature appended to this report. If they do so, I think they will find that it is clearly of a poisonous nature. It is not in any sense of a political nature but contains the poison of racial hatred.
There is another aspect of this matter not yet mentioned; that is the international aspect. In passing this bill, Parliament will be giving effect to the United Nations declaration on the elimination of all forms of racial discrimination passed unanimously at the UN General Assembly on November 23, 1963. Article 9 of the declaration reads as follows:
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
1.	All propaganda and organizations based on ideas or theories of the superiority of one race or group of persons of one colour or ethnic origin with a view to justifying or promoting racial discrimination in any form shall be severely condemned.
2.	All incitement to or acts of violence, whether by individuals or organizations, against any race or group of persons of another colour or ethnic origin shall be considered an offence against society and punishable under law.
Therefore, in 1963, on the unanimous recommendation of the nations of the United Nations, Canada undertook to promote legislation of the sort that we are dealing with here. I suggest that we are merely fulfilling our international obligations by passing this legislation.
I mentioned earlier that there were some modifications in this legislation that I wanted to see adopted. I want to speak about those at the present time. The first and most important modification that I suggest to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) and to the House is that instead of relying exclusively on
Criminal Code
purely penal consequences, such as imprisonment and fines, it would be perfectly proper and possible to introduce into this legislation what I call an injunctive process or a cease and desist order. This would be a far more flexible and far less penal method of dealing with this subject. If the minister has not considered such a possibility very fully so far, he might say that this is a civil remedy which is not open to us when we are dealing with the criminal law. I think the minister probably will recall-if he does not, no doubt some of his assistants will help him recall it-the Goodyear case which was dealt with under the Criminal Code and the Combines Investigation Act. In that case, the Supreme Court of Canada clearly and explicitly held that the injunctive process is a proper means of enforcing criminal law.

I appreciate the fact that the legislation must be based on criminal law to bring it within federal jurisdiction, but I am suggesting what should be an appropriate penalty. I suggest to the minister that to say to some offender who may be relatively innocent, an ignorant and misguided fellow, "look, you have made a mistake, don't do it again''' is better than putting him in jail or fining him a large sum of money. However, if he continued his actions, he would be guilty of contempt of court and a much more severe punishment would be justified. This injunctive procedure is more flexible.
Another reason for advocating the injunctive procedure is that once you have an injunction, it would apply not only to the accused but to his servants, agents and others working with him. Once you have an injunction against this criminal activity, you have the ability to enforce it and if some agent or servant continued the activity you would not require a further prosecution. I suggest to the minister quite seriously that this suggestion of mine deserves careful consideration. I offer it to him because I want to make his legislation work. I am not making the suggestion in a critical way, but I think it will reduce some of the sting of the legislation. As I said, I appreciate the necessity of dealing with hate

November 17, 1969
Criminal Code
propaganda under the heading of criminal law, but once you have it under that heading the type of remedy you choose makes a difference. It would be possible for the courts dealing with such cases under this injunctive procedure to do so in a more gentle fashion and not feel obliged to express their disapproval of the crime in question by a jail sentence or some heavy fine. It works the other way around also. A small fine may be considered a sort of licence fee, whereas a restraining order would have the whole majesty of the law behind it and would have to be obeyed. I hope the minister will consider this suggestion.
My other suggestion to the minister is to look again at the definitions. The British race relations act, which was passed fairly recently, requires a specific intent to stir up hatred against any section of the public distinguished by colour, race or ethnic or national origins. The word "wilful" is included in section 3. It is my view that the word "wilful" and the minister knows this very well-can be interpreted in many different ways by the Courts and sometimes means one thing and sometimes another. If you have to find a specific intent, as the British act specifies, to stir up hatred against some section of the public or identifiable group then, I suggest, you have an additional safeguard to those already in the act, and perhaps a better one. However, I appreciate that this discussion is one that can take place appropriately in the committee. I want to say to the minister that I prefer the British definition.
While I am referring to the British legislation, may I mention that some people have asked me whether we should not just rely on the common law and whether this type of legislation is not really unnecessary. One point that I would like to make in that connection is that this is a viewpoint strongly held within Great Britain. They have a long tradition of dealing with matters by common law and yet they found it necessary to bring in their race relations act, which is a parallel to this bill, and almost every thoroughly democracy, would adopt legislation of this similar provisions. I ask those who are so fearful of its effect on civil liberties to inquire whether countries like the United Kingdom and the Scandinavian countries, which have had a long tradition of civil liberty and democracy, would adopt legislation of this sort if it were truly a threat to civil liberty.
There is another suggestion which I should like to make to the minister which he might

consider at a later date. I think the working out of a law such as this one should be under constant review, and I hope that from time to time perhaps the parliamentary Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs would regularly review how this legislation is applied and how often the Attorneys General have been asked and have refused to act. I do not think this suggestion should necessarily be incorporated in the law but perhaps included in a statement of intent which the minister might give so as to relieve the fears of those who feel that perhaps this may be an invasion of our liberties. Indeed, if it turns out that this law is used as a cover to suppress legitimate freedom of speech or anything of that sort, I would be one of the first to say that it should be repealed right away; some such undertaking by the Minister might relieve the fears of those who are dubious about it.
Therefore, on the ground that there is here a clear and palpable evil which has reared its head in the country, on the ground that we are not in any substantial manner interfering with the freedom of speech, on the ground that the moral sense of Canadians requires this type of legislation, and on the ground of the educative effects of Parliament saying to our younger people, this racial hatred is abhorrent to Canadians, 1 urge this House to accept the bill.

Naturally, we want to condemn hate literature but, in practice, an analysis of the clauses of the bill makes us realize that what it proposes to do is very good, very noble and very commendable since, for instance, the purpose of section 267a is more or less to prohibit wars.
Even if Nigeria passed legislation against genocide, the government of that country would itself be accused of this crime!
November 17, 1969

How can the present government accuse itself of genocide against Biafra? I wonder. For this reason, I feel the first part of the bill aims at forbidding wars since genocide is committed particularly, during wars and generally, the belligerents in such conflicts try to exterminate one another.
This very pious measure, at least in that regard, seeks to prevent genocides. Of course, we are in favour of it in principle. However, what would it achieve?
I would like to point out some special aspects of the bill. For example, section 267a (2) reads as follows and I quote:
(2) In this section "genocide" includes any of the following acts committed with intent to destroy in whole or in part any identifiable group, namely:
(a)	killing members of the group, or
And this is the clause which I want to point out:
(b)	deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction.
The clause would have been more practical if reference had been made to moral destruction, because when the group is physically destroyed, nothing can be done to remedy the condition, since it no longer exists.
Moral destruction could occur and, then, we would have to charge ourselves with having caused, in a large measure, the genocide of the Indians and the Eskimos, because, from a moral standpoint, these peoples have practically been destroyed by our action during a number of years. It is therefore easy to see where this can lead us.
It is distressing and unfortunate to realize that such destructions, both physical and moral, can take place even in 1969. Evidence of this can be found in the wars now being waged in Viet Nam and Biafra. In principle, we are opposed to genocide.
It seems to me, judging by such comments, that the government is expecting some catastrophes to strike Canada in the near future. Which part of the country or what group of citizens are threatened with physical destruction, I do not know, but some catastrophes appear to be expected, and this bill practically marks the beginning of the end of the world.
In principle we agree to be against genocide but, as I tried to show, we consider that it is equivalent to day-dreaming, that it is a very nice bill, but a bill which does not really get us anywhere; rather it promotes distrust among Canadians, since it does not give us
Criminal Code
the opportunity to go to Biafra to solve the conflict. What have we to do with all this?
If I consider only the bill, I tend to think that its purpose is to prevent physical annihilation of the Indians and the Eskimos who are a part of the Canadian people. At first glance I do not see anything else in it. But, as I think it over, I say to myself: why should we try to stir up the fire, to add fuel to the fire at a time when the situation is such that the Quebec Minister of Justice is taking the bit between his teeth about everything and deciding when remarks are hateful?
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, the way things have been going for some time, anyone who dislikes the Quebec Minister of Justice will wind up behind bars. It is not under such circumstances that things should be stirred up even more and that such a bill should be introduced. Whom does it protect? What does it provide? In other words, what problem does it solve? Those are the questions I am asking myself.
I object to sections 267b and 267c of this bill for several reasons. I object to them because if they were strictly enforced, several among us would already have been indicted.
We have all been through election campaigns and we all know that in Quebec, particularly, they are sometimes waged in a rather unconventional way. Much hateful talking is done, depending on how this expression is interpreted. In a public meeting, it may happen that an individual's words seem insulting to someone attending that meeting to the point of causing violence.
Our Prime Minister himself (Mr. Trudeau) went through this. Is it possible for us to control the emotions, the feelings, the susceptibilities of the people attending a meeting? It is unthinkable!
Man as a free agent must assume responsibility for his actions and it is childish to let oneself be manipulated by some character trying to stir up violence.
How are we to interpret this piece of legislation? How are we to determine when a statement is of a heinous nature? Several persons will certainly have to suffer greatly from that situation, taking into account the succeeding political leaders. A statement will be considered heinous by some, and not so by others. Where will that lead us? This will create even more violence, if there is any. We must indeed agree on the meaning of that word.

There are at present great fears arising from certain things which are happening, particularly in Quebec. Such things have been happening at all times. I repeat at all times.
In my youth, I often heard political debates, during the famous contradictory meetings. They often led to lively fights. It has ever been so.
Nowadays, there are demonstrations, unplanned, but which nevertheless take place. We should not panic to the extent of opposing one of the most sacred and inviolable of rights, the right of speech, the right of the individual to express his opinion.
How many authors, even among the greatest, have promoted hate within the meaning of the law? It all depends on who hear them. When it comes to hate, it is important to make a distinction between the object and the subject of hate.
There is another matter which I would like to point out, and it is found at page 2. I quote:
(3) No person shall be convicted of an offence under subsection (2)
(a) for expressing in good faith and in decent language, or attempting to establish by argument used in good faith and conveyed in decent language, an opinion upon a religious subject;
There, the cat is out of the bag. An exception is made for a religious subject because it is expected that it is not this subject that may be the object of the enforcement of the law in Canada.
Yet if there is a subject which all through the ages has sown the seeds of hatred and .engendered religious conflicts and wars, that is the one! However, the law does nothing about it.
It is not necessary to go back very far in time, since in 1969 people still come to blows for religious differences.
Here, we eliminate this, even though paragraph 3 of section 267b appears to be somewhat less rigorous than preceding ones and I say "somewhat", because it seems to mitigate what comes before, and I quote:
(a) for expressing in good faith and in decent language-[DOT]
(i)	that the statements communicated were true, ,or
(ii)	that they were relevant to any subject of public interest, the discussion of which was for the public benefit, and that on reasonable grounds he believes them to be true.
How does one decide that public interest is involved? If a crowd of 4,000 or 5,000 gives a standing ovation to a speaker and that, afterwards, his words are called hate

propaganda by the Attorney General, what meaning should be given to "public interest"? Will a referendum be held each time to determine whether the public interest was involved? In my opinion, this question is extremely difficult if not impossible to solve.
This bill can lead to unjustifiable abuses. I am amazed that the Prime Minister, who not so long ago defended so strongly the cause of freedom, was seen with Michel Chartrand, for instance, inciting the Asbestos workers to resist the Quebec provincial police in the Duplessis era. I am surprised to see the Prime Minister forget his principles about human freedom, individual freedom, that he always fiercely defended.
For all these reasons, we cannot accept this bill as it stands now.
I repeat once more that we are obviously against hate propaganda and that, jointly with the federal government, we would like to eliminate, if possible, this kind of propaganda. But how are we to know What such propaganda is? Several cases, if not all, are already covered by the law. Indeed, if somebody feels he is being attacked by hate remarks he may always defend himself and this is what he does ordinarily.
I fail to see then the reason for this bill. It is too dangerous to accept it, especially in the present circumstances since it seems to represent a means found by the federal government to prevent I do not know what catastrophe in this country. I feel that it has a very poor opinion of Canadians whom I believe to be quite responsible. A few remarks judged hateful will not turn the people away from the real objectives to which must tend a society which considers itself "just" as advocated during the last session.
Hate propaganda really exists and I know it. Right now, the law even provides for the imposition of penalties in that respect because if the nature of hate propaganda were to be determined here, the so-called obscene propaganda would be considered to be the worst.
Obscene propaganda exists in this country. It runs free and, at the present time, abominable things can be read in the small papers published by students in high schools and in Quebec CEGEPs. Their material really amounts to hate propaganda; yet, nobody will curb it. Why? Because that propaganda precisely strikes at this country's fundamental principles, that is the Christian principles.
It is left to run free and, in consequence, we reach a point where we have to put up

Criminal Code
with hate propaganda of all kinds. Fortunately, the existing legislation is designed to preclude that, but nobody takes action.
The Postal service is sometimes used to dissiminate such propaganda; yet, some postal service regulations were enacted to check such occurrences. Nobody cares about that. On the other hand, if an individual dares promote a new political doctrine or question the constitution of this country, that is considered dangerous.
Mr. Speaker, if we ever witness the catastrophes that this bill seems to anticipate, they will be attributable to the excessive liberty we have allowed newspapers and writers, while the law provides penalties against such writings and the arrest of their authors.
I do not believe this bill will improve the situation any, but, it may offend a good number of people. As a matter of fact, this country will become more and more a police state and a dictatorship, something we all denounce and do not want to happen in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I understand that it is not the purpose of this bill to abolish hatred. I do not believe man will ever get rid of hatred and vengeance. I agree with the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) that racial hatred has reared its ugly head in this country and should be stopped, but I do not believe the purpose of this bill is to get rid of that very human instinct called hatred. Of all creatures, man alone has the instinct of hatred and vengeance. Curiously enough it is man alone who thinks he is more than animal. Man is the only creature who has the contention he is not animal, but something more than animal.
If Messrs. Martin and Fox, the United States anthropologists, Messrs. Martin and Forest, and Mr. Tiger from Montreal are correct, we must accept that racial differentiation, or at least the identification of groups, forms part of our civilization. It is not the purpose of the bill to create racial, ethnic or religious groups because these groups will merge and disappear. Even coloured races one day will merge into one.
Surely, the purpose of the bill is to protect the individual in a group so that the smearing, hatred and all that overshadows the whole group will not hurt the individual. We recognize this situation is bad for Canada. It is bad for national unity. It is an impossible 21362-57
and intolerable way of life. This bill has a purpose, but that purpose is not going to change, in general terms, the nature of man.
By law, we will restrict the use of communications and the printed word when they have no other purpose than to incite people to behave in an evil manner. Some hon. members have suggested this is not possible. Of course there will be many problems. The questions have been asked: What do we do with a child who makes statements? What do we do with the printed word? How do we define these terms? We will have many problems in deciding the application of this law, nevertheless throughout the history of civilization legislation has been very effective in controlling those instincts of man which do not contribute to civilized living.
With regard to vengeance, I am sure hon. members are knowledgeable enough in history to know that prior to the Samarian culture vengeance was unlimited. If you were a member of a neighbouring tribe and someone stole your property, you were at liberty to eliminate his whole family, tribe and even nation. This condition did not change until the Samarians enacted laws based on the principle of an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, which idea still prevails.
We must not consider legislation to be ineffective. It is effective. It proved effective in Ontario in the field of rental loans. At that time there were many complaints. The suggestion was made that legislation would never work because after all it was an interference with our individual liberty to rent properties as we saw fit. However, this legislation has worked. The majesty of law is very powerful if it is properly applied.
There is one issue I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. Although we have accepted the principle put forward that racial hatred and the dissemination of communications dealing with racial hatred shall not be used to the prejudice of any group, race or colour, nevertheless for some unknown reason we still accept the common law principle of truth as a defence. I am a lawyer. I have been trained in the common law. This great sanctity for the truth seems to be an excuse for everything. The minister should ask himself whether truth is an excuse for infringement of privacy.
Section 267b (3) states:
No person shall be convicted of an offence under subsection (2) .. .
(b) if he establishes
(i) that the statements communicated were true,-

Criminal Code
How many ways are there, Mr. Speaker, in which the truth can be used for the very purpose this bill is seeking to eliminate? Truths and half-truths have always been used by demagogues. Is it not true when certain people in the United Kingdom state their jobs have been taken over by coloured men from the West Indies? Is this not true? Of course, it is. Is the statement not true that in many large Canadian cities a certain professional group, or at least the majority of it, are of a certain religious belief?
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
What is the purpose of that? It is true, and under this bill the making of such a statement becomes an offence. It is the use of true statements, or the misuse of true statements which will make this law to some extent ineffective. There are more problems in connection with laws which contain loopholes than arise when there are no laws at all. Can the minister explain how anyone could be found to be prejudiced when he speaks the truth when one of the subsections provides a good defence if it can be shown his statements were relevant to any subject of public interest, the discussion of which was for the public benefit?
If anyone has a defence which establishes public benefit, surely he does not need the extra defence of truth. After all, the question "What is truth?" is one which will not be settled for generations to come. This will be the cyst which holds all the illness in the body of this legislation and will make this law ineffective since so much will depend upon the judge or upon the political temper of the times.
The common law concept is that no matter what you say, or about whom you say it, if you speak the truth you are exonerated. Nobody has questioned the reason for uttering these so-called truths. I would ask the minister and the committee to examine the sanctified word "truth" as it relates to a defence under this bill or under any bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I do not agree with this bill in its entirety, I do wish to make it abundantly clear at the outset that I see no reason at all why hate propaganda should be ignored. Discrimination of any kind on grounds of race, colour, religion or ethnic origin certainly cannot be tolerated. Any thinking person would surely agree with this view.
I notice that the bill omits the phrase "national origin" though it was included in the

report of the special committee as one of the areas in which discrimination should not be exercised. There is probably a reason for the omission of those words and perhaps the minister will take the opportunity to explain it when he comes to reply. I think it is agreed by all that in no circumstances must we allow the malicious abuse of any group, or person. The promotion of hatred constitutes without question a grave danger to our democratic system. Although the number of persons engaged in doing so may be relatively small, we cannot afford to ignore their activities.
I was interested and pleased to note on reading the report of the Cohen Committee that the promotion of hatred does not exist at all as a problem in my own province of Prince Edward Island. This is something of which I believe we can be justly proud; according to the committee there are only two provinces in which no such problem is encountered-the Province of Newfoundland and the Province of Prince Edward Island. I am very happy it is not a problem in my own province. Nevertheless, though it may not directly affect us, I wish to assure the House that I am vitally interested in the subject.
We all agree, I think, that we must be able to exercise maximum freedom of expression. But freedom of expression does not include the right to vilify or the right to defame. We agree with the Cohen Committee that freedom of expression is not an absolute right. The Canadian Bill of Rights guarantees freedom of expression to our people but at the same time we have laws which prohibit seditions, defamatory, libelous or obscene literature. Adequate provision is made in the Criminal Code to cover these areas.
Bearing in mind the principle that preference must always be exercised on the side of freedom of speech, I seriously suggest that when this bill gets to the committee we shall need to examine most carefully the question just how much speech is free speech. This is, in my view, the crucial question. As I mentioned before, those who advocate or promote genocide must, in my opinion, definitely fall outside the bounds of free speech; they cannot be protected by the argument that freedom of expression is allowed.
Turning to the bill itself, I note that clause 267a prohibits the advocacy and promotion of genocide. Genocide was, of course, prohibited under a convention of the United Nations ratified by Canada in 1952. This convention prohibited not only genocide but conspiracy
November 17, 1969

to commit genocide, attempts to commit genocide, and incitement to commit genocide. These things are already adequately covered. What the present bill attempts to do is to prevent the advocacy or the promotion of genocide. My chief concern is whether or not the intent of the whole measure is not already covered by the provisions of the Criminal Code as they stand.
I have examined the bill carefully, together with the corresponding sections of the Criminal Code, and I am convinced that the committee, when it comes to study this measure, will need to hear the testimony of experts as to whether or not all the things which this legislation purports to prevent are not already, with one exception, punishable under the Criminal Code.
It is interesting to note that in 1952, when Canada ratified the United Nations convention on the prevention of genocide, the then minister of justice, the Hon. Mr. Lesage, made the following statement before the Committee on External Affairs which was considering the subject in question. I quote from the report of the committee:
The opinion of the deputy minister of justice, which is accepted by the Canadian Government, is that the provisions of the Criminal Code as they are now, cover all the possibilities and are such that any of the acts mentioned in articles II and III are punishable under our law.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I suggest that it was obviously the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice in 1952, concurred in by the Minister of Justice himself, that all of the things that articles II and III of the convention attempted to do were adequately covered by the Criminal Code. I suggest to this minister-and I will make this suggestion to the committee-that quite probably the very provisions the bill attempts to make are already adequately dealt with by the Criminal Code.
Let me examine the bill to see whether I can make this point. The proposed section 267a provides as follows:
(1) Everyone who advocates or promotes genocide is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment-
The subsection goes on to provide a penalty of five years.
I suggest that section 407 of the Criminal Code makes the same provision. In fact, it goes further and provides for an even more severe penalty. I should like to place on the record the wording of section 407:
Except where otherwise expressly provided by law, the following provisions apply in respect of 21362-57|
Criminal Code
persons who counsel, procure or incite other persons to commit offences namely,
(a) every one who counsels, procures or incites another person to commit an indictable offence is, if the offence is not committed, guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to the same punishment to which a person who attempts to commit that offence is liable;-
Does that provision not cover the situation here? Section 267a provides that every one who advocates or promotes genocide is guilty of an offence and is liable to imprisonment for five years. The other section is differently worded; instead of "advocates or promotes" the wording is "counsels, procures or incites". Why cannot a man who promotes genocide be charged under section 407 of the Criminal Code?
I think the committee should look into this question, because if a man can be charged and convicted under section 407, the penalty is more severe than that provided by the proposed section 267a.

The hon. member is anticipating me; I intend to deal with that point. I agree the section does not deal with group defamation, and so on. However, I am dealing with the case of the individual. My argument is that the proposed section 267a provides imprisonment for every one who advocates or promotes genocide. If the committee receives expert testimony that convinces the members of the committee that the words "advocates or promotes" carry a different meaning from the words "counsels, procures or incites", then it may be that section 407 would not conflict. But there seems to be very little difference between the wording. As I say, a man charged under section 407 with incitement to commit genocide can be convicted under that section regardless of the provisions of section 267a.
Let me now deal with the proposed section 267b, which provides:
(1) Every one who, by communicating statements in any public place, incites hatred or contempt against any identifiable group where such incitement is likely to lead to a breach of the peace, is guilty of
(a)	an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years; or
(b)	an offence punishable on summary conviction.

November 17, 1969
Criminal Code
Under that provision the choice apparently rests with the prosecution whether someone is charged with an indictable offence or with an offence punishable on summary conviction. In the latter case, the accused is not entitled to trial by jury, to be tried by his peers. I think a person charged with an offence as serious as this should be guaranteed the right to be tried and judged by a jury, rather than by a judge or magistrate alone.
I suggest that this provision in the bill is also included in the Criminal Code. Bearing in mind that the proposed section 267b provides that every one who, by communicating statements, incites hatred or contempt is guilty of an offence, section 160(a)(i) provides: Every one who
(a) not being in a dwelling house causes a disturbance in or near a public place,
(i) by fighting, screaming, shouting, swearing, singing or using insulting or obscene language ... is guilty of an offence-
In essence, is this not the same provision as the proposed section 267b, which refers to persons communicating statements-in other words, speaking-in a public place that incite hatred or contempt? Section 160 uses the words "insulting or obscene language". I suggest that insulting or obscene language would in all probability lead to the inciting of hatred or contempt.
This is another point on which the committee must hear the opinion of experts. It is my firm conviction that anybody charged under the proposed section 267B could just as effectively be charged under section 160(a)(i) of the Criminal Code.
I come now to the proposed section 267b (2), which provides:
Everyone who, by communicating statements, wilfully promotes hatred or contempt against any identifiable group is guilty of
(a)	an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years; or
(b)	an offence punishable on summary conviction.
As has been pointed out, this is a new provision. That is what is described by the Cohen committee as group defamation. We have not anything in our present law which covers group defamation. That section, as it is presently drafted, is to me a very dangerous section, and herein lies the danger. It provides:
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Everyone who, by communicating statements, wilfully promotes hatred or contempt against any identifiable group is guilty of (a) an indictable offence-

Let me point out that the communicating statements do not have to be made in a public place. In other words, if I made such statements in my own home, I would be liable to a charge under this section. Surely, the minister would agree that the section is wide enough to include what I might say in my own home in the presence of my own family. Surely, that is dangerous. It has been said here many times that the law has no place in the bedrooms of the nation. Certainly, it has no place in the living rooms of the nation.
I do not think we should restrict expression of opinion so drastically that we cannot express our opinions within the confines of our own home. To be liable, as I read it and I am subject to correction by the minister, what I say does not have to be said and what I do does not have to be done, in a public place.
Even more serious is the penalty section. What may happen to me if I do say something of this nature within the confines of my own home? Subsection (4) of this proposed section reads:
Where a person is convicted of an offence under Section 267a of subsection (1) or (2) -
It is subsection (2) of this section which makes it an offence to say these things in your own home. Let me repeat what it provides:
Where a person is convicted of an offence under Section 267a or subsection (1) or (2) of this section, anything by means of or in relation to which the offence was committed, may, in addition to any other punishment imposed, be ordered by the presiding magistrate or judge to be forfeited to Her Majesty-
Does that mean if this offence is committed in my home that my home is liable to seizure and forfeiture to Her Majesty? It says "anything by means of or in relation to which the offence was committed". If the offence was committed in my home, then it is in relation to my home that the offence was committed and there is a possibility that my home could be seized. The minister smiled, but I am sure this is not a smiling matter. There is some reason for looking carefully into this provision.
Surely, the minister and members of the committee will agree that this section as it is worded could prevent me from free discussion in my home or free expression of my opinion to the members of my family. I suggest further, and again I am subject to correction if I am wrong, that subsection (4)
