imposes a very heavy penalty when it provides that "anything by means of or in relation to which the offence was committed" may be seized and forfeited to Her Majesty. The section also indicates, and this is a very clear departure from the present law, that this type of defamation includes spoken words and gestures. What is meant by the word "gestures"? How do I offend against this law by gestures?
Another provisions of the bill with which I strongly disagree, and this has been mentioned this afternoon, is that part which leaves it to the discretion of the Attorneys General of the provinces whether or not an offence should be prosecuted. This is wrong and the discretion should not be left with the Attorneys General. Certainly if I were an Attorney General I would not want to have to shoulder that burden. I am confident that if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) polled the Attorneys General of the Provinces he would find they prefer not to have that burden placed upon them, and they would make that decision for obvious reasons. The Attorneys General are subject to all the vagaries of politics and, if they can avoid it, do not like to cause ill will or discontent among those they perhaps later on will have to turn to in search of support at the polls.
The Cohen committee has indicated that this Provision is included to avoid frivolous and vexatious prosecutions. I seriously suggest there is another very effective way of preventing frivolous and vexatious prosecutions. The magistrate or justice of the peace before whom one goes to swear an information and complaint, if he fulfils his duties and does what he is required to do under the Criminal Code before signing such a document, would make inquiries as to the circumstances surrounding the alleged offence. If he felt that the charge was vexatious or frivolous he would choose not to issue that information and complaint by simply saying: No, I am sorry, but in this case the circumstances as they appear to me do not warrant the issuing of such a charge.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jerry Pringle (Fraser Valley East) moved:
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF QUALIFIED PERSONNEL AT AIRPORTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the govern-, ment should consider the advisability of making regulations, pursuant to paragraph (r) of section 273 of the Customs Act, so as to facilitate airplane tourist traffic at Canadian airports of entry by providing for the deputizing of qualified personnel now employed as management or administrative officers to handle customs clearance to such tourist traffic.
He said: Mr. Speaker, during my submission to the House of Commons today I hopefully propose to provide sufficient information regarding Canada's general aviation industry to lay a base for the support of my motion to recruit airport managers and their assistants to act as customs officers to handle customs clearance for flying tourists at airports of entry.
I know from personal experience that the vast majority of Canadians are unaware of the volume of light plane traffic using Canada's air space today. I refer to light planes as single engine and multi-engined, propeller, turbo-prop or jets capable of carrying from 2 to 15 passengers per aircraft. Their access to air space while travelling east and west is relatively unhampered. However, southbound traffic across the border and return has been and still is seriously handicapped by lack of customs and immigration service at non-airline and non-international airports of entry.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I hasten to state categorically at the outset that under no circumstances should my statements be construed as a criticism of our Canadian customs and immigration officials. I

November 17, 1969
Customs Act
am confident that I can say without fear of contradiction that allowing for a few minor exceptions we receive courteous and efficient service from customs and immigration officials. I congratulate both the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cote) and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mac-Eachen) on their personnel officers charged with the responsibility of selecting staff who daily serve the Canadian public. Perhaps a short explanation regarding international aircraft tourist travel would serve to acquaint hon. members with some problems which could be resolved by the adoption of this motion.
Aircraft returning to Canada or United States aircraft coming to Canada are required to file flight plans at points of departure in the United States. The intended Canadian port of entry and estimated time of arrival are stipulated, plus request for customs clearance The flight plan is passed to the Department of Transport radio service office nearest to the port of entry. The Department of Transport notifies the local customs officer who endeavours to meet the aircraft on arrival. It is unnecessary for the pilot to clear with United States customs when departing from the United States. There is a similar situation the other way. This system worked well at international airports and reasonably well at airports of entry where customs offices are located nearby during the period when seven day per week clearance was available at all points of entry. This is no longer the case. The average time involved in clearing an aircraft is less that 15 minutes. However, travel to and from airports is time-consuming and Inconvenient. Nevertheless, aircraft tourist traffic has steadily increased during the past number of years when customs clearance was available on a more or less sunrise to sunset basis. The nominal mileage fee paid by the pilot has been acceptable to flying tourists.
How many of us realize that more than
12.000	United States airplanes visited Expo '67? During the Abbotsford Air show, held annually in August, 1,400 aircraft from the United States visited Canada for the three day event in 1969 alone. In Canada today there are 10,000 registered aircraft. Light aircraft account for all but a few hundred. However, when we look at our tourist potential the figures are most impressive. There are
700.000	licensed pilots in the United States. Of the 130,000 registered airplanes in the United States, 98 per cent are owned by general aviation or non-airline people. The Federal Aviation Administration in the United States

estimates that 50 per cent of all air passengers in the United States are carried by nonairline airplanes. Therefore, flying tourist traffic offers great potential, but lack of customs clearance assurance at Canadian ports of entry, other than international airports of entry, discourages our United States friends from travelling to Canada in light aircraft.
It is true there was a time when only the idle rich could afford private airplanes. This concept is no longer valid. Canadians and Americans in all walks of life are registered owners and pilots. The flying farmers association utilizes various types of aircraft as operational vehicles to facilitate emergency trips to centres for repair parts, fence inspections, aids to round-up of cattle, crop spraying, and so on. Since most airports are located some distance from the urban centres, the general public is unaware of the ever increasing light plane traffic. In fact, light plane traffic has been increasing so rapidly during the past few years that governments, in their wisdom, have been endeavouring to entice light airplane traffic away from major international airports in the interest of easing congestion. Governments have also been increasing aid for development of smaller airports in both urban and rural areas.
It should also be pointed out that light planes can be equipped with navigational and radio aids equal in sophistication to those on the largest jet transports. While this is most helpful on cross-country flights, approaching and landing procedures at large international airports can become congested as a result of the wide difference in speed between light aircraft and jet transports. Light plane pilots appreciate the policy of the Department of Transport to build and improve more small airports. This allows a pilot to elect to avoid high density areas. The recent reduction of customs service to smaller airports of entry must therefore be considered to be in conflict with government policy.
I am sure we all commend the government on its recent policy of taking positive steps to reduce government spending. We can readily agree to the abandonment of costly projects as commanding lower priority to essential services. It is not my intention today to suggest that revisions of regulations in respect of customs and excise to downgrade essential custom service to the Canadian public should be reinstated. On the contrary, my motion, if approved, would provide an alternative which would not only serve to upgrade customs clearance service at airports of entry, but would do so without-and I emphasize this-
November 17, 1969

additional cost to the federal treasury. Mr. Speaker, the flying public's greatest concern centres around the fact that the alternate proposal of providing service from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. five days per week is unrealistic.
Flying tourist traffic reaches its peak between Friday afternoon and Sunday evening. During a discussion with the vice-president of American Owners and Pilots Association, I was advised that, in his opinion, American pilots will avoid trips to Canada as a result of the recent change of policy. Service on week ends is available at a few large airports but is available to most airports of tourist destination only on payment of heavy travelling fees. One airport in my constituency which has provided unlimited customs service for the past 20 years is now denied service after 5 p.m. and on holidays, Saturdays and Sundays.
If a pilot arrives a few minutes late or inadvertently files a flight plan requesting customs service after 5 p.m. he is forced to pay more than $22 for not more than 15 minutes attention. The amount represents travelling mileage cost from the closest automobile port of entry. No wonder the vicepresident of AOPA, representing over 500,000 pilots in the United States, is of the opinion that Canada will be on the taboo list for American flying tourists.
On September 9, a well known executive of Smith Falls, Ontario, attempted to land at his home airport after filing a flight plan from his departure point in the United States requesting customs clearance. Radio contact informed him that the local customs official was unavoidably detained and unable to clear him even though he was arriving during the prescribed period. This situation forced him to continue his flight to Ottawa for clearance and he lost an hour of valuable time, plus the additional cost of aircraft operation.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Similar incidents are being reported daily across Canada. Aviation associations are presently appraising the damage to our flying tourist trade as well as complaints of unfair treatment resulting from the arbitrary downgrading of service by the Department of National Revenue. They are also pressing the industry to find an alternative. I submit that this motion could very well serve this purpose.
True pioneers spawned and developed aviation throughout the years. Obstruction to normal aviation has been in evidence since Orville Wright got off the ground at Kitty
Customs Act
Hawk. The aviation industry is conditioned to opposition and has been travelling upstream for years. It is now conceded that modern aircraft are the safest, fastest and most reliable means of transportation today when calculated on a passenger mile basis. Sophisticated navigational and pilot aids have reduced the accident rate well below any other method of travel in proportion to passenger miles. The air passenger explosion has been astronomical, and governments throughout the world are endeavouring to decentralize airports and control zones to accommodate the increasing number of daily arrivals and departures. Some uninformed officials advocate elimination of light planes in the airspace. This attempt will be as successful as a similar one would be to ban automobiles from highways in favour of buses and trucks, even though the high incidence of accidents on highways would indicate more justification for a ban.

speechtext:
I previously mentioned that aviation is the offspring of pioneers-pioneers who have never been satisfied to rest on their laurels. All fliers and those associated with aviation have an inherent desire to assist development whenever and wherever possible. It is, therefore, only natural that when a problem arises seriously threatening development, the industry seeks to find a logical and practical solution. The excellent co-operation of the Department of Transport notwithstanding, there are those of us who feel that the accelerated aviation development, other than that of airlines, took place more in spite of government intervention than because of it.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your indulgence in permitting me to lay the foundation in support of my motion. The industry now

November 17, 1969
Customs Act
stands ready to suggest to Parliament a solution which could alleviate problems relating to customs clearance at most airports of entry.
Practically all airports of entry are owned by cities or municipalities or a combination of both. Airport boards of directors employ managers and assistants to collect fees and rents, to supervize airport maintenance and safety regulations, and generally to act as policemen of administration. Their duties are usually performed between sunrise and sunset. The men and women so involved are responsible people, more than capable of handling the very limited requirements for customs clearance of non-commercial aircraft and I stress the word "non-commercial". I am referring to tourist aircraft. They are already gainfully employed at airports and are oriented to performing and enforcing disciplinary rules as set out by the Department of Transport and civic authorities. They would be ideal customs officer deputies who would faithfully perform their duties as prescribed by oath on a seven day per week basis. Travelling costs between customs offices and airports would be eliminated. These officers would be subject to periodic inspection and would be responsible to the closest customs office where regular reports could be submitted. Customs officers would be relieved of the inconvenient trips to airports during office hours, which would improve their office efficiency.
I reiterate that there would be no added cost to the federal treasury. The actual time required to clear tourist aircraft is usually less than 15 minutes.

speechtext:
I will be glad to answer the question after I conclude my speech in a minute or two. Should costs be incurred, the existing user charge for custom officers' transportation would probably cover them.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I sum up my points for the consideration of this House.
First, the anomaly of forcing light aircraft to clear customs at busy international airports of entry at a time when the Department of Transport is encouraging pilots to use smaller airports is ludicrous.
Second, in view of the fact that many nontrained personnel such as university students are now being deputized as customs officers

during the busy summer months, any argument that a precedent would be established is nullified.
Third, American flying tourists intent on visiting Canadian outlying areas would be able to plan their flights on a more practical direct route which would aid the economic development of small centres.
Fourth, the reduction of customs service which has recently taken place at a time when aviation activity is on the increase is a severe deterrent to Canadian tourist trade.
Fifth,, a survey of airports of entry in Canada indicates that many growth centres will suffer needlessly unless this motion is adopted and implemented. The number is impressive but I list a few of the cities which will be in trouble, such as St. John, N.B., Quebec City, St. Jean, Quebec, Smiths Falls, Brandon, Regina, Saskatoon, Florenceville, Swift Current, Lethbridge, Cranbrook, Castle-gar, Penticton, Chilliwack, and Pitt Meadows. Areas such as Portage La Prairie in Manitoba are now severely handicapped inasmuch as Winnipeg is the closest airport of entry.
There are many more points I would like to raise but time does not permit. I submit that the aviation industry stands ready through the many administrative officers to accept the challenge of participatory democracy. Responsible Canadians are prepared to serve this government and assist in reducing the heavy costs of governing. The practical approach suggested in this motion in no way reduces the effectiveness of customs and immigration control. On the contrary, the proposal contributes to increased air safety, now uppermost in the minds of us all.
A challenge is also presented to Canada's civil service, one of seriously placing the needs of the people of Canada in a priority position. It is my sincere opinion that the public service will rise to the occasion in the interests of essential services to Canadians at the grass roots level, and support my motion now before the house.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the proposal put forward by the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle). I think it is an excellent one. However, I do not want to get caught in the crossfire between two government supporters. But I do wish to say that I am completely at a loss to understand the reasons behind the interruptions of the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. All-mand). Undoubtedly later on he will explain just what is bothering him. Perhaps he did not pay too much attention when the hon. member for Fraser Valley East began his address.
1 believe that the mover of the motion has raised an important point. It is not something earthshaking, but if adopted his proposal would be beneficial at a lot of smaller airports. I go further to suggest that at airstrips in northern parts of the provinces officers of the Lands and Forests Department might very well be deputized to handle customs matters.
As the hon. member for Fraser Valley East has said, the volume of tourists coming from the United States, particularly by air, is increasing. I know this from personal experience with the Muskoka airport. At the present time, it is served by a customs officer stationed in the nearby town of Bracebridge. When an incoming small aircraft from across the border intends to land there, the pilot must notify the Canadian customs of his expected time of arrival. Then, the customs officer has to close down his small office in Bracebridge, hire a taxi to take him to the
airport, and often has to keep the taxi waiting for 15 minutes to an hour until the aircraft lands and he has fulfilled his duties.
The result is that the incoming pilot has to pay a considerable amount for the transportation and waiting period of the officer in order to get customs clearance. In some cases when he has nothing to declare, the whole procedure is a waste of time. Yet he has to pay the bill for the time wasted. During this period the local customs office is closed and regular customers must wait for the return of the customs officer.
I see no reason why local people at such airports could not be deputized to handle customs matters. On a recent trip overseas I was quite amazed on landing at London, England, to find two doors in the arrivals area, one with a notice on it "Articles to Declare," and the other with a notice, "Nothing to Declare." It just happened that I had nothing to declare and so I went through the second door. I looked around for somebody to whom I could declare nothing. There was no one there but a sweeper. I asked him, "To whom do I make my declaration". He said, "You came in through the door "Nothing to Declare" and I said yes. He said, "Well, go on." To my mind this was a very strange situation, but it has an interesting parallel.
I do not know the percentage involved, but I do know that a large number of people passing through customs have nothing to declare, especially people who come into Canada in small aircraft. It is a waste of time to have a customs officer attend at an airport just to have some person say, "I have nothing to declare." At Muskoka airport the customs officer is doing his job as well as he can, but often he has to explain to irate, incoming tourists why they have to pay a bill for customs officer's transportation even though they have nothing to declare.
For some two years Hammond Transportation has been applying to have a customs warehouse for both highway and air transport authorized at Bracebridge, but for some reason or another the Department of National Revenue has been very hesitant about the matter. If anybody at all in that department happens to read the report of this debate, and I trust somebody will, I hope he will look over the file of Hammond Transportation and decide on this customs warehouse. It would be a great convenience to tourists.
There is another side to the coin, Mr. Speaker. For some time I have been hearing complaints at various conferences about

United States tourists who come to Canada in light aircraft which land on lakes in the northern parts of the province. These tourists then set up hunting and fishing camps, having brought in their own provisions and supplies. When they have completed their hunting or fishing, they head back to the United States without ever seeing a customs officer. As I say, this is not an occasional thing. It is becoming so serious that many hunting and fishing outfitters are concerned. Further, people interested in conservation are concerned at the catch which these people take out of the country.
This traffic is not all illegal because in most cases there is a Lands and Forests man in the area from whom they can get hunting and fishing licences. But having done that, these people feel no further responsibility to this country, and are of no benefit to it. We do not know what they bring in or what they take out. If a Lands and Forests officer were deputized to take customs declarations from these people, the situation would be covered. It would remove the fear of illegality or improper action with respect to hunting and fishing parties.
In the province of Ontario there is now a program to provide landing strips. In many cases these are just landing strips on a piece of level ground, with only a windsock as equipment. This program is designed exactly for that situation. In many cases lands and forests agents are present and could carry out the necessary duties in legally admitting people to the country and taking their customs declarations. They could also deal with people when they were leaving.

I support completely the hon. member's notice of motion and think there is a perfectly good case for someone on behalf of the government standing up and saying that the motion will be accepted. I for one, and I think I speak for many of my colleagues, agree with this proposal. It is not a bill, but a resolution expressing an idea. Few notices of motions are accepted. I think this is a very good one which ought to be accepted. Departmental officials would know that the House of Commons is interested in this matter. If departmental officials want to draft the legislation differently, I suppose no one would object. I think, Mr. Speaker, that this 
is a perfectly good example of a notice of motion which ought to be accepted.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a rather interesting debate. Perhaps it is not as earth-shattering as the debate that will develop with respect to the white paper on tax reform or debates wherein our foreign and defence policies are being reviewed. This debate deals with a facet of Canadian life which is of interest to many Canadian people. Perhaps it does not command the attention it deserves. The hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle) is indeed a pioneer of the air age. Had he been born in another generation, I am sure that today he would be halfway to the moon. I think he has made a most imaginative proposal. The discussion that has surrounded this proposal has been most interesting and enlightening.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka (Mr. Aiken) suggested that lands and forests officials could be used in the province of Ontario. I might tell the hon. member that in his own constituency there is a lake-landing facility with customs facilities operating from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. As I found out to my discomfort this summer, R.C.M.P. are also stationed there. When they are available, they also could fill this role. That would be very interesting because these men are federal officials.
I do not think we realize the effect that operators of small, private aircraft are having upon our economy and society. I am particularly interested in the comments of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka with reference to small aircraft operators from other countries poaching our fish. As a fisherman, I fear these people entering Canada. There are hundreds, possibly thousands of poachers using our virgin lakes in the north and I resent the fact that they are stripping these lakes.
There is another element of this question which concerns small aircraft. I refer to the bush pilot who is part of our Canadian heritage. This facet of Canadian development was exemplified recently in a movie starring James Cagney. These small aircraft are vital to our north. I am referring to the new frontiers in our northlands where there is noother means of transportation. The motion

November 17, 1969
Customs Act
before us deals with the people who operate these small aircrafts which are vital to opening up the north. This is also of vital importance to our tourist industry. A facet we seem to have overlooked is that which has built a great portion of the small aircraft industry in the United States. In this respect they are perhaps a generation ahead of us. Industrial expansion in the United States has to a very large extent moved out of the northeast corridor. The New England textile mills have moved into the south, the petrol industry has moved from Texas into the mid-west and the great national and international corporations have established branch plants near their raw materials and markets. The officials of these industries must commute by small aircraft. This is part of their everyday life. It does not affect everyone. Those who are dealing with far-flung businesses and have experience with the private jet or propeller aircraft and appreciate them. The private or corporate aircraft is a very important part of our industrial complex.
Canada is embarking upon a program of regional economic expansion. We should bear in mind what the hon. member for Fraser Valley East has said because he is opening up another facet of this program which will be very important to us. There is not much point in spreading our industries into the Mari-times, remote areas of Quebec, Ontario, the western provinces and even as far as British Columbia without providing the facilities with which to make them operative in the twentieth century. This is an important fact that we should not forget. We will be spending hundreds of millions of dollars to upgrade industry in outlying areas. This is how it should be. We must recognize the fact we are living in the latter part of the twentieth century. We have to deal with the communications systems that exist, of which private and corporated aircraft are a very important part.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING HATE PROPAGANDA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate was adjourned at five o'clock I was relating what I conceived to be some of the dangers inherent in the bill, particularly in proposed section 267b. I pointed out that according to my interpretation of this provision its terms were wide enough to prohibit me as a private citizen, within the confines of my own home, from inciting even the members of my immediate family to hatred or contempt of any kind. I feel that this would be a very serious infringement of my privilege of free expression. I would agree that statements inciting hatred of any kind should certainly not be allowed to be expressed in public. On the other hand, I submit, and I propose so to argue very strenuously before the committee, that this provision should be restricted to statements made in public, and that I should be allowed to speak as I like within the confines of my own home.
I am supported in this contention by a statement made before the Senate committee that was studying the precursor of this bill on

April 22, 1969, as reported in report No. 7 of the Standing Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs of the Senate at page 148, in a brief presented by Professor H. W. Arthurs, who was at that time, and I presume still is, Associate Dean at Osgoode Hall Law School of York University. This man is very learned in the law; he made a very complete study of this matter prior to appearing before the Senate Committee, and I suggest his opinion should be given some weight. This is what his brief says regarding proposed section 267b of the Criminal Code:
Subsection (2) is also open to serious objection. There is no limitation as to the time, place, or circumstance of the communications which are forbidden. Surely we do not wish to come to the point where casual conversation, or even formal communication, within the confines of a selfrestricted group becomes a matter for regulation . . . The section, as drafted, invites snooping, an informer system, and ultimately an awareness by each citizen that words spoken by him may be reported to "Big Brother".
This is the danger I see in regard to this provision. I quite agree that a restriction of this kind has no place in casual conversation within the confines of a self-restricted group. I suggest to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), and I will so suggest to the committee, that this section as drafted would be a very dangerous provision for Parliament to enact. Furthermore, as now drafted the bill is open to the interpretation that as soon as a police officer thought that a speaker at a public meeting was saying something that could possibly be considered as incitement, he would have authority under the bill to intervene and force the speaker to withdraw. I think that is a reasonable interpretation of this particular provision, and I contend that conferring such power would be very dangerous.
I have every respect for police officers. In many cases they are doing their best to carry out what is a very difficult job. But let me warn the House of the danger of giving police officers too much power. Despite the fact that most police officers are sincere, human nature being what it is there is a danger that they may not exercise with discretion the power conferred upon them. The Criminal Code provides that any person who, by speech or otherwise, incites a disturbance of any kind is subject to the penalties provided by the Code. But the big difference is this: under the Code a person must incite a disturbance, whereas under the terms of this bill a police officer in attendance at a public meeting has it entirely within his discretion
November 17, 1969

to stop a speaker proceeding if he thinks that such continuance might incite the audience.
I do not have anything more to say about the bill, Mr. Speaker, other than this. While we on this side of the House agree for the most part with the principle of the bill and are prepared to give it very close scrutiny in committee, I am not at all convinced that the present provisions of the Criminal Code do not already adequately cover the ground this bill is attempting to cover. Some may ask: "Well, what if it does? What harm is done if we also pass this bill?" To that argument I would reply that we must not clutter up the statute books of Canada with duplicate legislation.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Heaven knows, the Criminal Code is already in bad enough shape in many respects; it is archaic, outmoded and outdated. I even venture to recommend to the Minister of Justice that he get to work as quickly as possible on revising the Code so that these outmoded, archaic and outdated provisions are removed. They are a source of confusion, and any lawyer practising today will confirm that our Code is cluttered by things that have absolutely no significance in present day circumstances. It would be a very serious mistake to enact another law covering something that the present Code covers; things this bill purports to cover. For that reason we propose to give the bill very close scrutiny in the committee. We will insist that expert evidence be presented to us in order that we may be convinced there is no duplication.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING HATE PROPAGANDA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, five years ago this month I was invited by the late Hon. Guy Favreau, then Minister of Justice, to become a member of what was formally appointed in the following January as the Committee on Hate Propaganda. At that time I was appointed to the committee. I was of the opinion that hate propaganda was not a very serious matter, if only because no reasonable person could take it seriously. I think it worthy of note that at that point I had never seen a piece of hate propaganda.
Subsequently, as a result of the work of the committee, along with other members I closely examined hate materials of a great many different kinds and variations that had been distributed in Canada. We studied the data of social psychology which made us aware of the effect which abusive and hateful material of this kind could have on society. In the course
Criminal Code
of our studies we naturally also reviewed the law. As a result the committee unanimously recommended to the Minister of Justice that certain changes be made in the Criminal Code of Canada. These changes are reflected almost exactly in the bill now before this House.
There are a few changes from the recommendations of the Cohen committee in the bill now before the House, but they are not matters of great importance except where they improve the bill, such as the additional requirement for the approval of the attorney general before a prosecution can be brought. In all major respects the bill and the recommendations of the Cohen committee are the same.
It is not a good idea to confuse political and legal truths with eternal verities, and I am hesitant to say anything which may sound that way. However, as a result of my experience, I believe that any person who approaches this subject with an open mind, and sees the material to which the committee was exposed, and holds the same basic value position, that is, that civil liberties are not absolutes but are to some extent modified by the rights of others in societies-I believe anyone who approaches the subject in this way will come to the same conclusion that we as members of the Cohen committee came to some five years ago.
The thrust of this bill is the creation of a legal concept of group defamation. All the clauses of the bill fit in, in some way or other, with this concept. In its purity, if I may put it that way, it is found in the definition which is described as the wilful promotion of hatred to be found in the proposed section 267b (2) of the Criminal Code. It is also found with some modifications in the offence described as public incitement of hatred. Group defamation as described by that definition must take place in public and must be such as is likely to lead to a breach of the peace.
This principle is also found in the offence which is described as advocating genocide. This section does not prohibit that which is prohibited in the Criminal Code, that is, murder; it does not prohibit the killing of an individual or members of a group. It prohibits a certain kind of advocacy or promotion of an idea which is intrinsically vicious, an idea that is often identifiable with the hypothesis that a possible solution to our social problems is the killing of members of a social group in whole or in part. It is the advocacy or promotion of this idea which the government

November 17, 1989
Criminal Code
proposes to make illegal by the Criminal Code of Canada.
This is also within the concept of group defamation. It goes beyond our normal understanding of that concept because it not only defames the group-there is defamation because the promoters of genocide would say a group was so unworthy and hateful it did not deserve to live any longer. It goes beyond the notion of group defamation to include the idea of killing, but it reflects the basic purpose of the whole amendment by incorporating the concept of group defamation.
It is interesting to note that the common law does not contain a concept of group defamation. Traditionally, of course, we have had an offence of defamation. It has been a matter for civil action. Defamation has, also, throughout the history of the common law involved a criminal action, one which could be brought by the state against those who defame others. I include both libel and slander when I use the term "defamation". Traditionally, the common law did not in this respect apply to a group. Those whose minds the common law reflected did not believe that it hurt a man when you said something about his group. Individually he could be hurt and his reputation could be ruined; therefore, he could be seriously affected by something which was said against him as a person. That is, if it were said that an individual was a liar or a dishonest man, this was something that could reflect on him. But if he was a member of group "X", and the statement was made that all the members of group "X" were liars, thieves, prostitutes or whatever, in the view of the common law this did not touch the individual.
It is now clear, in light of the new discipline of social psychology, that this is simply not true. We now know from our studies of society, and of individuals who have been adversely affected by a denigration of their group, that what is said against a group is something that is said about a man himself. It may not affect him directly, and its effect may depend on how directly he associates himself with his group, but what is said about his group affects him as well.
Our group associations are deep-seated and, naturally, as far as the individual is concerned, depend upon his tradition and upbringing. Social psychology can no longer, as the common law suggested, support the view that group defamation does not matter. We thus know from recent science that group defamation is a very serious thing indeed.

The interest, one might even say the right- although it does not yet exist legally-of a group, quite possibly a minority group, not to be defamed or to have their persons affected by what might be said about them as members of a group, should be protected.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
There is a real deficiency in the law. It simply does not take account, except in very tangential ways, of the members of a group. Some authorities believe that if a group is as large as 20 people the law might go that far, but when it becomes a multitude or a significant group in our society it is not protected. Therefore it is no exaggeration to say that our law, as it is now, really is not aware of group defamation.
We have an interest to be protected which is not now protected in our legal system. This would suggest that some protection should be put into the law. Before we can come to that conclusion with any certainty we must, as the Cohen committee did, look at the other side. We must see what adverse effects could result from inserting a concept of group defamation into our law, because any change made in our legal traditions could have a considerable effect on many aspects of our life. It would be foolish to assert that such legislation as this would not in some sense infringe on free speech. This is obvious, and was fully accepted by the members of the Cohen committee. Then the present offence of criminal defamation has the effect of limiting the free speech of an individual. Of course, all such offences have only a subsequent effect in that the act is committed before the penalty is attached. In other words, there are not prior restraints nor should there be. Yet it is quite reasonable to say there are limitations on free speech, because if there is anything men cannot say in social or individual dialogue without a legal consequence, then their liberty is infringed.
Is it wise to have this type of legislation which infringes on our existing freedom of speech? We cannot answer that question, I submit, unless we consider the other side of the question as well. We have a situation in which, while a man cannot slander another as an individual, he can do so as a member of a group. It is only by looking at the two interests which are to be protected together that we can hope to come to a reasonable solution.
I admit that if we introduce the concept of group defamation into our law, this would represent a greater curtailment of freedom of
November 17, 1969

speech than exist in the present law of criminal defamation. I would admit this because it appears to me that when one speaks in a more general or universal sense, which is the way normally one would speak about a group-the very notion of a group suggests that one must make a generalization about it and not just refer to a particular incident involving a particular individual-you get close to the area of philosophical thought, political generalization or religious opinion and argument. One then has gone further into generalization, so that there is a greater danger to free speech from a concept of group defamation than from a concept of individual or criminal defamation.
The fact, however, is that the legislation proposed to this House contains safeguards of a kind which have never been found in the common law. It was because of the greater danger to freedom of expression which occurs with the concept of group defamation that the Cohen committee recommended these safeguards. For example, the common law never had a defence of truth per se to a concept of defamation. It was never a defence to excuse yourself by saying something was true-civilly it was, but not criminally. This bill proposes that a person who can prove to the satisfaction of a court that his statements were true is exempt from any legal liability.
This legislation which would offer more than the traditional protection of the common law reads as follows:
(i)	that the statements communicated were true, or
(ii)	that they were relevant to any subject of public interest, the discussion of which was for the public benefit, and that on reasonable grounds he believes them to be true.
I would be the first to admit of subsection (ii) that it is not crystal clear, and undoubtedly the members of the committee in their consideration will look at all such details of this bill. It is, however, the traditional statement of the common law in statutory form in our present Criminal Code. It is the one which in respect of criminal defamation has been found to give more or less adequate protection to the interests of freedom of speech.
In addition, this bill provides-and this is new provision over and above the recommendations of the Cohen committee-a further exemption for a person who expresses in good faith and in decent language, or who attempts to establish by argument used in good faith and conveyed in decent language, an opinion upon a religious subject. The whole realm of
Criminal Code
religious opinions, provided they are held in good faith and expressed in decent language, is exempt from the effect of this bill.
These are very considerable limitations upon the possible scope of the bill, but in my opinion they are limitations which are fully justified and which indeed are made necessary by the very desire to protect to the widest feasible extent the freedom of expression which truly is a very important part of our democratic heritage. Similarly, in respect of the offence of public incitement of hatred there are protections. These protections have not been noticed, I might add, in all of the discussion which has revolved around this bill. Recently, for example, we had a newspaper editorial-I do not seem to have the editorial but I can refer to it from memory- to the effect that if at a recent hearing of the Gendron commission someone had uttered a word of English, because the audience was composed of French-speaking people who were in a very hostile mood toward the English the speaking of the word of English and the consequent uproar would make the utter-er of the word of English guilty of an offence. This is the sheerest nonsense.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
First of all, it is rather unlikely that this type of group will be protected. The type of group which is under the protection of this legislation is distinguished by colour, race, religion or ethnic origin. The government has dropped the notion of "linguistic group" which the Cohen committee suggested should also be given protection. It has also dropped the notion of "national origin" which was recommended by the Cohen committee for inclusion in the definition of the protected group. But much more important, any utterance which would lead to liability has to be one which would objectively, that is to the mind of the reasonable man, be considered to be one inciting hate or contempt, one which is viciously abusive of the opposing group.
It is true that in England in the Burgoyne case the court, interpreting similar legislation, held that you have to take the crowd as you find it and that the crowd is not subject to the test of a reasonable man, so that if you say something which will disturb one crowd and not another you will be guilty if you say it before the more volatile crowd. But that applies only if what you have said is itself objectively abusive. If it is not objectively abusive, if it would not be abusive to the

November 17, 1969
Criminal Code
mind of a reasonable man, no liability is possible. That is why so much of the interpretation which has been given to this section and so much of the argument which has surrounded it has been wide of the mark. As a matter of fact, if I may draw the attention of the Minister of Justice to this, there is a section in the Criminal Code which does not have the same protections. It is section 160 which reads as follows:
Every one who ... causes a disturbance in or near a public place, by ... using insulting or obscene language,... is guilty of an offence punishable on a summary conviction.
It does not apparently have the same type of protections with which we have surrounded this bill. The section on genocide also well protects the interests of any who are concerned that their freedom of expression will be reduced by this bill, because here we see the operation of the broad section of the bill defining the group which is protected, which as I have mentioned is any section of the public distinguished by colour, race, religion or ethnic origin.
It must be a Canadian group, "a section of the public"-that is the Canadian public -and only such a section of the public which is distinguished by one of those four qualifiers. The definition of genocide is also extremely limited. Of the five-part international definition, three parts of which were retained by the Cohen committee in their recommendations, only two parts now remain in the bill which is before us. They include an act of killing members of the group or one of deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction. Much of the argumentation which has revolved around this proposal related to the earlier version of this bill which was introduced in the Senate, but the bill was amended there and is now presented in its revised form to the House.
There are those who feel that a government which is as dedicated as was this government last year to keeping the law out of the household, out of the domestic community, is being inconsistent if it proposes in another bill to make illegal something such as the distribution of hate propaganda which would conceivably occur in private circumstances- not of course under the public incitement of hatred charge, but under the wilful promotion of hatred section. It is argued that the state should have no role therein. I do not believe that anyone has ever contended that there is any area of human conduct which is completely exempt from the reach of the law. It

is pretty obvious that if there were a murder in a house this act would fall under the present criminal law of Canada.
The question to which we must address ourselves is, what is the public interest even in a situation which may be a relatively private one: is this a matter in which there should be a continuing public interest or is it a matter which is better left to the disposition of the parties involved? I believe that there is such a public interest in the matter of hate propaganda. I believe this because it is indeed a serious matter.
Some critics of the Cohen report have said that the distribution of these materials across Canada has not been so very wide after all, only some 20 or 30 communities have been affected. They have been among our largest cities, but only a limited number of cities have been affected and only a limited number of people have even seen hate propaganda. One of the special techniques of the purveyors of this horrible material is to send it to the members of the group which is being attacked-not to distribute it to the public at large but to seek out deliberately members of the Jewish or Negro community and to send the material to them.
Some have thus argued that because of the limited distribution of these materials and because of the limited number of years over which distribution has occurred-although it is continuing and we have no reason to think it is going to stop-because of the limited number of people who have been involved in its distribution, and because indeed of the limited number of different hate publications, this is a matter which is not serious. I dispute that view.
This is a serious matter, not perhaps quantitatively but certainly qualitatively. It is a serious matter because of what it may do to brutalize the sensitivities of the majority group to the feelings of the minority. Over a period of time, as a result of the constant distribution of this kind of material, it may make the majority unaware of the feelings of the minority. In some cases it may indeed be sufficient further to inflame an already prejudiced majority against a particular minority, at least in a particular community.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
But it is not the effect on the majority of the public which is the most serious. What makes hate literature so intrinsically awful is the effect which it can have on the minority group, the fact that as a result of a constant series of encounters which involve hate
November 17, 1969

propaganda-and indeed which come as well from other sources in a society-a group can be made to feel completely unworthy, completely inhuman. We know, from what we now see in the United States, that when a group is thus affected its reaction may turn into aggression. When this happens, obviously the problem is brought very forcibly to our attention. When the negroes, a group which has been subject to so much of this vilification in the United States, rather than turn the other cheek turn to violence, this is when our society sits up and takes notice. At this point the majority can no longer ignore the feelings which the minority have.
But, Mr. Speaker, instead of turning to aggression, which makes the matter clear to all of us, the minority can turn within itself; it can retreat upon itself; it can be affected internally; it can be affected in such a way that it is unable to function properly in society. I would not want to build up a case which suggests that these hate materials are the only cause of this kind of effect in our society. Obviously this is part of a larger problem which the institutions of law cannot deal with completely. Hate propaganda is not the whole problem of hating. Law is not the only solution to hate in our society. But hate propaganda is an important part of the problem and law is one of the most effective ways in which our society can deal with it.
This is not only because of the effect of law itself through proscribing a particular offence, through making it go underground if you will, though if the law does this it achieves its purpose in part because if hate material goes underground and ceases to be circulated the law has achieved what it is trying to do. But it is not only the punitive effect of law which is important; there is also the educational effect. If the punitive effect is not justified, the law would not be justified for its educational effect alone. But given the validity of the punitive effect of the law, which I believe is here amply justified, the educational effect must not be ignored.
In this law we have an appeal to the conscience of the Canadian people, an appeal to all of us to put our convictions in writing, in the Criminal Code of Canada, to make them part of the moral code of our society and to display them in a way which will be plain not only to ourselves but also to those of the minority group who may be attacked by less well informed and less well intentioned members of society.
I submit in conclusion that in this age we can no longer ignore psychological effects. We
Criminal Code
can no longer think that the law has to deal only with the obvious things. This is an age which is becoming increasingly more subtle, and the means both punitive and educational by which the law deals with social problems must also grow in subtlety. This bill, I submit, is an example of a new subtlety in the law.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING HATE PROPAGANDA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I most certainly agree with the statement made this afternoon by my colleague from Greenwood that Bill C-3 is entering into a very sensitive area of legislation. I believe that I fully understand and appreciate the motive behind the introduction of this bill. I feel absolutely safe in saying that every member of this House despises the dissemination of hate whether it is by voice or by writing. However, sir, having said that I have some doubts about the application of the bill should it become law.
I believe there are some questions that need to be answered, some problems upon which we need more information. I am one of those who think that you cannot legislate hate from the minds and the hearts of mankind. I am one of those who believe that in order to completely eliminate hate from mankind we will require in our country a change in environment, in atmosphere, and indeed in the form of society itself.
I believe this is similar to the fact that you cannot legislate out of the minds of some people a desire to gamble, a desire to smoke cigarettes or to enjoy alcoholic drink. Admittedly, we do have legislation that tries to control certain aspects of gambling and the use of hard liquor, so I assume that the purport of this legislation is to try to control the dissemination of hate attitudes and literature. But there is a difference between trying to legislate control in the sensitive field that we are now discussing and trying to do it in the field of gambling, etc.
Some of the questions which I think have not been answered are: just what is the line of demarcation between liberty and licence? What would be the line of demarcation as to what would be permissible and what would not be permissible in the individual or collective expression of a strongly held point of view, whether by voice or by demonstration?
I imagine the answer would be, "The decision will be made by the attorneys general of our country, and by the judiciary." That would not satisfy me, Mr. Speaker, because in the past we have known attorneys general to give different interpretations of the same law. Just prior to the amendments we made to the

November 17, 1969
Criminal Code
Criminal Code last session I do not believe there were two attorneys general in Canada who made the same interpretation or took the same action with respect to such a simple matter as the law dealing with bingos and raffles. Of course, when it comes to the judiciary there are examples galore of how different judges interpret the law. On the one hand you may find a man who has stolen millions being fined-that being nothing more than a licence to steal-being given a few months in jail or two or three years in the penitentiary. On the other hand you may find a hungry man who has stolen a loaf of bread receiving a suspended sentence or being punished with the full weight of the law. These differences arise from differences in interpretation and application of the law. Often we find that judges in different parts of the country hand down different sentences for similar crimes committed in similar circumstances. I hope, and I believe others share my hope, that sentences will be meted out and decisions handed down according to an accepted principle, and that these sentences and decisions will not vary from coast to coast.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
It is important for us to consider the question of hate. Hate is not new in our society; it arises from antagonisms and to some extent from policies of governments. Those policies engender the antagonisms which sometimes develop into hate. Indeed, how can one forget that a quarter of a century ago the Japanese in our country were uprooted, interned and not treated as good citizens. Their assets were sold at give-away prices. Nevertheless, in this country at that time not one Japanese was found to be a spy or saboteur. But the government's policy engendered antagonism and hate.
I see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) looking at me. I remind him that not too long ago we had in force a quota system governing the entrance to Canada of immigrants from many countries. Many who lived here were unable to bring in their loved ones, even though they came from some part of the famed British Commonwealth of Nations. Need I remind hon. members that until a few years ago the Chinese, East Indians and native Indians of democratic Canada did not have a vote. The government has a responsibility in this field, because antagonism and discrimination are the forerunners of hate Luckily the circumstances I have alluded to have now changed. Government policy has changed; there is no longer a quota system,

and citizens of various countries desiring to be admitted to Canada have the right to apply for admission and to be considered. Under our federal law all people except those who are under 21 years old or who are state wards in insane asylums and penitentiaries have the right to vote. Having lived in Canada since I was three years old, I have become convinced that with the change in government policies and the removal of prejudice and discrimination, a new attitude has dawned among our people. By removing discrimination we have removed those antagonisms that lead to hate. Those words apply particularly to ethnic groups as well as individuals.
During my childhood, and indeed up until a few years ago, one could note the existence of antagonisms and hate on Canada's Pacific coast. For instance, an Italian was a Dago, a Chinese a Chink, a Japanese a Jap, a Scandinavian a Bohunk and a Catholic a Dogan. Such terminology applied to human beings brought about an atmosphere of antagonism and hate.
In the last few years the use of these terms, in my area of the country at least, has died out. Very rarely do you hear now such terms used. The result is that we live in a better atmosphere. A better environment has brought with it a lessening of hate. I feel certain that these great advances have been made through education and understanding, and that greater advances will be made in the future. Eighteen months ago hardly a week went by when I did not receive despicable and vicious hate communications. By invoking a section of the Post Office Act dealing with scrurrilous literature I was able to stop the flow of some of this literature. Now I can say that I have not had a letter of this type for the last year-not one. That leads me to believe that in our country we are experiencing a greater degree of human feeling, understanding and brotherhood. For that reason I think we ought not to tackle this matter so much by legislation as by education.

speechtext:
We will solve this problem by improving the national environment and atmosphere. I believe that education is as important as legislation in this field. Instead of asking our attorneys general and our judges to make decisions in these areas, we would be better employed in trying to bring about greater intermingling between the various ethnic groups in this country. Let us try to avoid isolating ethnic communities, even in
November 17, 1969

our urban areas. I believe most strongly that you cannot do those things by legislation alone. If we want to counteract the effects of antagonism and hate in this country, let us stop calling ourselves English Canadians, French Canadians, Italian Canadians, Chinese Canadians or Japanese Canadians. Let us call ourselves Canadians.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING HATE PROPAGANDA
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING HATE PROPAGANDA
speechtext:
In that way we can do more good in this country than we can by any legislation.
It is because of my feelings in this matter and because I have the honour of representing a riding which contains the largest number of ethnic Canadians west of Toronto -a riding which contains thousands of Italians, Chinese, Ukrainians, Scandinavians and people of Germanic origin-that I find myself in a somewhat difficult position this evening. Because of the views I have tried to express, I hesitate to support second reading of this bill. At the same time I recognize that there still exists a problem. I recognize and appreciate the motive which is activating the Minister of Justice. Because of this I do not feel I can vote against the bill.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Hon. members will understand how great my interest will be in the hearings, discussions and deliberations of the standing committee of this House of Commons to which this bill will be referred. I hope the committee will not only consider this bill but all aspects of hate and the dissemination of hate. I hope as a result of its deliberations a recommendation will be made to this House which will include the two suggestions of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), namely, the injunction policy and a policy of committee review if this bill becomes law so that judgments can be made on the experience gained from its application. We will then learn whether the bill has provided the right approach to the problem.
I do not have a closed mind on the issue before us. It is one of great concern to us all. I hope the minister and the government will be amenable to the suggestion of a full study by the committee. I hope some thought will be given to policies of greater education, integration and achieving more understanding among our people. Some hon. members might feel I am indulging in wishful thinking and idealism, maybe cliches, platitudes, generalities or whatever term they like to use but, Mr. Speaker, I feel most intensely that the
Criminal Code
solution to this violent, vicious problem will only be achieved by a changed environment, atmosphere and society. Each and every one of us should do our part in expressing two main points of view. First, a wonderful way to abolish the attitude of hate by an individual or a group is to place less emphasis on preaching the principles of Christianity and to start putting them into practice; second- and this is a repetition of what I said-in the final analysis the solution to the problem is a recognition that irrespective of where we were born, our colour, race or religion, the future of Canada relies upon our being proud that we are Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Haidasz (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING HATE PROPAGANDA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the representative of the federal constituency of Parkdale, within whose boundaries live many people who suffered persecution because of their race, religion, ethnic or national origin, and whose relatives and friends were victims of genocide, I consider it my duty to participate in this debate.
During this discussion on Bill C-3, amending the Criminal Code and indeed strengthening it to deal with the dissemination of varieties of hate propaganda, I wish to commend the government, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) and his predecessors for proposing this legislation. We also owe our deep gratitude to those of our colleagues who have served in this House and the other place, to all organizations, churches, writers and individuals in our country who have clamoured for and supported the principles of this legislation.
For those who have survived the Nazi concentration camps and for those of us who have visited these camps or who have firsthand contact with people who have suffered racial, ethnic or religious persecution, this legislation has not come too soon. After visiting the Nazi concentration camp of Auschwitz with some of my colleagues from this House, I cannot understand the indifference of so many people, especially those who have tried to delay this legislation and those who are indifferent to the victims of Nazi persecution.
There are still many people in our country who suffer the effects of the tortures, persecution and the memories of an evil society that failed to exercise its conscience in the face of moral perversion. While many have suffered because of anti-semitism, I wish to emphasize that hate propaganda affects Canadians of all origins. If anything, recent

November 17, 1969
Criminal Code
history has taught us that racial hatred and inter-group hostility cannot be confined within tight limits, but appears to be frequently seeking new targets.
The terrible risks of anti-racial incitement, while at present directed only against a few groups are a threat to all Canadians. It is no exaggeration to say, Mr. Speaker, that however confident we are of the strength of our democracy, any hate movement, if it is not stopped, bears within itself a potential threat to our society. While we may feel certain that the healthy fabric of our democratic society will be able to withstand the assault of hate propaganda, surely our citizens have the right to protection against this affront to basic human dignity. Canadian citizens should be able to live in this country without being submitted to vicious baiting and incitement which is degrading to the whole concept of the human personality. A just society must be able, through law, to offer its citizens at least this minimal protection and safeguard.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Every law is in some way an encroachment on certain freedoms but I believe Canadians as a whole have been ever conscious of the need to preserve their precious heritage of liberty, freedom of speech and freedom of expression. Only in the context of such freedom shall we be able to preserve our society from the disease of hatred and prejudice which can destroy our nation.
Bill C-3 follows several pieces of legislation introduced by Canadian governments and enacted by the Canadian Parliament to protect human rights and the dignity of the individual. I believe this bill discharges Canada's obligation to the United Nations convention on the crime of genocide which was tabled in this House on March 2, 1950, and approved by resolution of both Houses in 1952. This law and others like it will not eliminate those whose twisted minds lead them to sow hatred and spew the venom of racial prejudice and hatred. Such despicable behaviour and thought are symptoms of racial tension. I consider this lunatic behaviour to be a dangerous poison which must be eliminated.
We should seek out the causes of such behaviour and eliminate them as soon as possible. In this task, education in good citizenship and devotion to the principles of justice, tolerance, mutual understanding and respect are necessary. Every Canadian must look into his conscience and be ever vigilant against the subtle infection of prejudice; our
[Mr. Haidasz.l
happiness and survival as a nation demand it. That is why this evening I should like to appeal to all in the chamber to support the legislation now before us, to make sure it gets a good hearing in committee and, finally, to approve its passage in this House.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING HATE PROPAGANDA
speechtext:
I want to say a few words on this bill, Mr. Speaker, because of the importance which it obviously has, and because, like so many others in this House, I have studied for some years the problem with which it deals. I want to begin by saying that I greet with pleasure the concern evident all around this chamber about the infringement of freedom of speech and freedom of assembly. 1 think I can say that the members of the party to which I belong, those who will sit on the committee which is to consider this bill, will enter into the discussion with open minds and a determination to support any reasonable additional safeguards, if such are proposed, to make certain that the bill cannot be abused in such a way as to abridge freedom of speech or freedom of assembly, provided this does not hurt the objectives which this measure seeks to realize.
To all hon. members who have spoken along this line, and whose judgment I respect, and to all those who gave evidence before the Senate committee on this bill, whose judgment I respect, I want to say we should not allow ourselves to be blinded by generalizations in such a way as not to deal with abuses of freedom which threaten civilized behaviour and the social fabric of a civilized society. There is a danger-and certain episodes in recent history have shown this to be the case-that genuine democrats become so complacent about freedom and democracy that they permit those who are determined to destroy freedom to abuse the democratic rights and eventually to cast down democratic society itself.
There is a great deal of talk about whether or not the present criminal law is adequate. I am not an expert in criminal law, Mr. Speaker, and I do not pretend to be; my legal practice has been in another field. Nevertheless, I have read carefully the report of the Cohen committee and the appendices to that report, and I have had occasion over the last number of years to read the opinions of eminent lawyers in the criminal field all of whom are agreed, as the report puts it at page 40:
In sum it is evident that the Criminal Code even on the widest interpretation does little or nothing to protect groups from the evils of hate propaganda.
November 17, 1969

I suggest that these studies and this conclusion are sufficient at least to cast doubt on the assumption that the present law covers the situation. Since there is doubt about it, surely one cannot oppose an attempt to clarify the situation and remove that doubt by enacting specific legislation to deal with the particular subject with which we are concerned.
The other point I wish to make is that as a matter of fact, and this is surely important, a great many civilized democracies in the world have enacted this kind of law-LAW-countries and societies which respect freedom of expression and freedom of assembly just as much as we do, and which have found it necessary, particularly since the end of the second world war, to take action along these lines. I have in mind the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, France, Norway, Switzerland and the United Kingdom, to mention only a few, all of which have introduced legislation to deal with group defamation and the spreading of hatred based on race or religion or ethnic origin.
My fourth point is that we have an international obligation to pass a law similar to the bill which is before us. As the hon. friend for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) pointed out, on November 21, 1963, a United Nations declaration against discrimination was adopted unanimously. Canada was there, and voted for it. Article IX of that declaration-my hon. friend read part of it-required member nations to take immediate and effective measures, including legislative and other measures, to prosecute and/or outlaw organizations which promote or incite racial discrimination or incite or use violence for reasons based on race, colour or ethnic origin. We voted for this declaration. We gave an undertaking that in our own country we would make laws along these lines. If I remember correctly, the convention concerning genocide, adopted in 1949, was ratified in both Houses of Parliament in 1952. In that convention on genocide, articles IV and V require the contracting parties to undertake to enact in accordance with their respective constitutions legislation to give effect to the provisions of the convention and in particular to provide effective penalties against persons guilty of genocide or any of the other acts enumerated in article III.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I do not say this is conclusive, but it seems to me that one of the things we suffer from in this world is this: Members of the United Nations vote for international conventions and for international undertakings; this
Criminal Code
implies that member states should do something to implement such undertakings. Nevertheless, when the representatives at the United Nations return home, nothing is done in this regard. This is one of the evils of the present situation that we ought to rectify. Having undertaken these international obligations, I would suggest to hon. members that we have a duty to carry them out.
I wish that this kind of law were not necessary. I wish I could share entirely the optimism of my hon. friend and colleague from Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). However, it has been my experience, perhaps because I am a member of one of the minority groups affected by hate propaganda, that racial and religious prejudice is present in most people just beneath the skin and that it does not take very much to evoke some active expression of racial or religious prejudice.
I forget exactly when, but some months ago one of the Toronto papers took a survey of school children at high schools and public schools in Toronto and found there was a disturbing and widespread form of racial prejudice against Negroes, Jews and other minority groups. So I suggest it is a mistake to assume that this kind of prejudice cannot exist in Canada. I am confident that under present circumstances in the world today

I say this without reservation-Canada is one of the freest of communities and societies. Its society is less cursed with the kind of active and overt racial and religious prejudice that is existent in other societies. But it is a mistake to be complacent about this. It is a mistake not to realize that it is there none the less. This curse of racial and religious prejudice is present in our society today. The hon. member for Vancouver East indicated in his speech that the expressions "Dagos", "Japs", "Chinks", "Sheenys" and "frogs" have now disappeared. With all respect to the hon. member, I wish what he said v/ere true, but it is not.
Too often one finds it is possible for the best of people with the broadest of outlook to give expression to the sort of thing that feeds racial prejudice and religious antagonism, and this sometimes unconsciously. I have been in the company of people who were aware of my origin, and some of the "best" people in the gathering made jokes about the Jews, or about the "niggers", or somebody else, which shocked me because I was sensitive to this sort of thing. No doubt they would not raise anything to hit me on the head; I have no fear of that. Nevertheless it is a fact-every

November 17, 1969
Criminal Code
member of the House who is objective about this knows it to be a fact-that our society is not yet clear of this sort of prejudice. Our society is still full of the sort of antagonism that is based on racial, ethnic and religious grounds, and these antagonisms are transmitted to our children. There are teachers still in our schools who are guilty of this sort of thing; it has not been eradicated.
My thinking on this subject has always been affected by personal experience in the early 1930s. At that time I was studying in England and had occasion to visit Germany as a student. At that time I spoke German fairly fluently. I visited various parts of Germany and saw what was happening there, particularly in the summer of 1934. When I returned to Oxford and made some speeches about what I had seen, people in the audience would frequently come up to me and say: "Oh, come on, David! Don't exaggerate. The Germans are cultured people, highly educated. They are a scientific race. Sure, this crazy guy Hitler has been promoting these ideas, but the majority of the German people cannot possibly accept them. How can a cultured people that nourished Goethe and Beethoven accept this kind of nonsense?"

majority.
