speechtext:
The great, silent majority, as someone at the back suggests. All this is history now. 1 think no country can boast greater tolerance than Great Britain, but even in that country it did not require much immigration of coloured people to have a minister of the Crown defeated on that very issue, as was Patrick Gordon Walker. There have also been near-riots as a result of this kind of racial discrimination.
When 1 returned from England in 1935 and made the same kind of statements to people in Canada, I got the same reaction. Such a suggestion was incredible. The fact is that decent people have not the evil imagination that can conceive of the kind of terrible things that happened in Germany, or that happen in South Africa or Rhodesia. Although we read about them and understand the situation, it is very difficult for us to conceive, in our feelings and in our emotions, of people acting in this way. However, history has shown that people do act in this way.
Some 30 or more years ago a book was written by a great theologian and teacher of ethics in a Christian seminary in the United

States, and I am sure the name is familiar to all members of this House, Reinhold Niebur. The title of his book is "Moral Man and Immoral Society". The thesis proposed by the book, which has been proven sociologically time and again by history, relates to what an individual in his own home and in his private behaviour may not be prepared to do but who, if he is a member of a mob in a certain sociological and economic situation, will do such things. The evil that is in him will come to the forefront as a member of the mob in a way that would never happen when he is merely a private citizen. Social conditions which produce that kind of expression can occur in any country, including this great country.
I ask hon. members to take every precaution possible to defend freedom of speech and freedom of assembly. Let us take every precaution possible to prevent the abuse of legislation so as to abridge such freedom unnecessarily and unjustifiably. But I beseech hon. members not to sit complacently in their seats and think that in this great Canadian society we do not need to worry about this problem, because we do. If we are to build a genuine, even better civilized society than we have now, we must deal with this matter. I make no apology for saying that I know of no greater social evil than racial and religious prejudice and intolerance. There is no greater evil.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I can and do criticize the social evils in our society that are derived from economic inequality, from social inequality, from inadequate treatment of the poor and from the great, and I consider unnecessary, concentration of economic and with it of political power in the hands of a group that is not responsible to the people. All these are evils against which, with or without the approval of the majority of the people in Canada, some of us have fought all our lives and will continue to fight. These are evils derived from society as a whole. They are not equal to the vicious evil which is racial prejudice, racial antagonism, religious prejudice and religious antagonism. I say this as dramatically as I know how, Mr. Speaker.
No society can ever be quite civilized so long as there is in it that kind of prejudice and intolerance. Who could disagree with the eloquent and relevant language of my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East, who said that education is more important
November 17, 1969

than this law? I do not disagree with that and I do not think anyone could. Obviously you cannot legislate hatred out of people. You might be able to legislate other things, including some of the things he mentioned, but you certainly cannot legislate hatred out of people. You can do that only as society improves its environment and its administration and as our educational system does its job more adequately for our children. This situation will continue a couple of generations before that end can be accomplished, and I hope it will be accomplished in years to come. There is value in legislation, none the less.
I would be surprised if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) claims for his bill the attribute that it will solve the problem of racial discrimination or the spread of hatred. I am sure he does not claim that. I am sure he is as aware as the rest of us that much more will have to be done in society. But there is value in legislation, particularly in legislation which takes the necessary safeguards against abuse. I should like to mention three obvious results of good legislation along this line. The first relates to those people who follow the leadership of hatred peddlers. Among them are a good many people who are innocent and decent but have been sold an idea. I have met many of them at my doorstep in the religious sphere. I have met some of them who are anti-Semitic and I have met some who have talked about the negro in a manner in which it is uncivilized to speak. Many of those I have met are not really vicious people; they have been sold a bill of goods and have accepted it.
I suggest that legislation on the statute books will tell those otherwise decent and law-abiding citizens who have been sold a bill of goods that what they have been doing is contrary to the moral sense of the society in which they live, and is against the law. Many of these people will simply quit because it is against the law, and that is what the law is for. That is the first obvious consequence which is desirable in any society.
The second thing is that those who have no regard for the law, and those who will not be influenced by an appeal to morals in our society, will have the dissemination of this literature stopped by law. The third and equally important result of legislation like this is what several members, and most eloquently if I may say so, the hon. member for Greenwood pointed out, namely, the educative value of the presence of the law on the
Criminal Code
statute books of the country. If we enable the teachers of the country to point to this law in the classrooms, there will be great educational value to it. The hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) also stressed and emphasized this important point.
Finally, I say that every law can be and has been abused. I know of no good law that has not known abuse in the past, and I imagine none in the future will ever know the lack of abuse. We have the Unemployment Insurance Act, a piece of social legislation obviously of importance to people who are unemployed, but it has been abused. It has been abused by people who take advantage of the law and by those who administer it whose hearts were often in the wastebasket and whose heads were somewhere else than on their shoulders. One can think of no law, no matter how good, which has not been abused by administrators, by the judiciary, by lawyers and by citizens of the community.
However, the possibility of abuse should not stand in the way of a law which is socially necessary and desirable. This should make us do everything we can to provide all possible safeguards against the likelihood of abuse. Having done the best we can, we ought to pass the legislation and make it the law of the land. I wish this kind of law were not necessary in Canada or anywhere else in the world, but I am afraid I am pessimistic enough to think it will be needed for some years to come.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be quite brief. Many fine arguments have been advanced in favour of the bill. I shall not repeat those but will add one more. I have been pleased to study the bill, and I have read a number of letters from various groups. Some of those letters expressed the fear of an invasion of private rights; others contained imagined reasons for fear, and still others showed or contained sheer emotional nonsense. I think all these people are entitled to be reassured, and for that reason I now speak.
I cannot see anything to be concerned about. The bill intends to curb the intended activity of an individual by making it a crime to make a vicious attack on a group. This bill is an attempt to prevent a criminal act which is about as anti-social as any activity could be, and I have noticed that those who oppose the bill do not come from any minority group.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Let us hope it will never be necessary to use this new legislation or the power provided by it; or if this does become necessary, let us hope that very seldom shall we have to use this power. Surely in a nation as advanced as Canada the time has come to state in the form of a statute that we stand very firmly against such behaviour. If we do this we may lead the way for other nations.
I support the bill. My only regret is that it does not go further and supply some restraint against those who recklessly, and often with venom perhaps because of their own distorted thoughts, attack individuals. The bill covers certain groups. The individual is not covered. At times an individual is unable to defend himself, perhaps because of his position in society or because he cannot afford the expense of fighting a libel action, if that should be a sufficient means of fighting back.
When a man's reputation has been destroyed, is it good enough to say to him that he can institute a libel action and perhaps receive a judgment in the amount of $5,000? We must realize that many of those who would attack someone in this way usually are judgment-proof; in other words, the judgment or assessment cannot be recovered.

I suggest that today the libel action is obsolete in respect of protecting a man's reputation. There was a time when if a person committed slander or libel he was faced with paying a lawyer and proving his statements or paying damages. Today the situation probably is that the man who is libelled pays a lawyer and commences an action, while the man who was responsible for the libel is carried by legal aid and thereby does not pay. If he does not have any money, he is unable to pay a judgment against him. The person who has been libelled has been involved in a great deal of time and expense in defending himself.
This is one step, but I believe we must take the next step. Bills have been presented in this House to the effect that we should compensate victims of crime. Is it any worse to lose an arm or have your reputation destroyed by one of these hate dispensers who distributes libellous publications? I suggest to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) that 1969 is not too early to draft legislation with sufficient sophistication that it will protect people who are attacked in this manner and at the same time not take away the civil liberties of honest people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of taking part in this debate, but certain remarks made in the house prompted me to give my opinion on BiU C-3.
To begin with, I must tell the house that I am not a lawyer. I feel that our laws would sometimes be better if we took into account some of the comments made by the public at large.
I would like to say something about certain remarks made by the previous speaker. He discussed an aspect which is not covered by this bill, namely the protection that the law must provide for the individual who is a victim of libel, slander or statements which affect his reputation. This bill is incomplete because it does not mention the kind of libel and slander that can be made against an individual.
In his speech, the previous speaker said, and I quote from memory:

If the character of the person is destroyed, the judgment passed by the accuser is not correct, or something of this sort.
November 17, 1989

'Translation]
I readily accept the hon. member's statement, because it reminds me of the misfortune which beset a whole family. The reputation of a prominent Canadian was affected, and the result was to ruin him as a public figure. Also, the reputation of a family highly regarded in the province of Quebec and throughout Canada was greatly prejudiced. It is with regret that I recall here the unfortunate Munsinger affair. It offers an excellent opportunity to show how little legislation takes into account the individual and the protection it should vouchsafe him against libel and defamation of that kind.
As we all remember, documents of public interest were involved. We all know the name of the citizen whose political and personal reputation was attacked and destroyed, I am afraid, for the rest of his life.
That was one of the most painful things we have experienced in the history of Canadian politics. What is intolerable is the reason for which use was made of this man, with a world-wide reputation in the military field, who had earned the world's most valued decorations during the last war. The man was painfully and cruelly wronged in his reputation. His family suffered greatly and his life, both social and private, was unjustly affected.
In my opinion, this bill should have been the opportunity for the minister and the government-allegedly seeking the just society and the protection of the citizen's basic rights-to provide adequate protection not only to the groups defined in the bill but also to the individual.
Hon. members will recall that when the Munsinger affair broke out, the desired objective was not only to tarnish a man's reputation but also and above all to destroy a political party.
While I refer to that matter, I do so with much restraint. I do not intend to attack anyone, but this incident shows that if the minister had readily wished to respect the basic rights of the individual and to protect him against defamation, he could have provided in Bill C-3 some protection against that kind of abuse.
By the way, I should like also to refer to defamation which is often in the form of cartoons. During his political career the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) as well as other people may have been the victims of cartoonists working for newspapers or magazines
Criminal Code
who very often use their talents to circumvent the law relating to defamation or even the bill which is now before the House.
I have seen in newspapers cartoons directly attacking the reputation of some people. And since the law is made in this way, the authors of such cartoons could not be prosecuted because it could not have been proven that there had been dishonest intent.
The minister should really take note of these remarks that are not made in a legalistic spirit, since I am not a lawyer. But my experience in political life has perhaps taught me a few things, and I think the minister should certainly amend his bill or else make some recommendations to the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, in order that this aspect of the problem of libel and defamation be thoroughly examined.
It is quite easy to kill a political man, an opponent or a personal enemy through the use of cartoons and, in this way, get around the law and avoid the penalties provided in this bill or in any other provision of the Criminal Code which deals with libel and defamation.
I had not intended to speak for any length of time, but I owed it to myself to make these comments. And I think it is unfortunate that the minister has restricted the application of Bill C-3 to some groups, when, in my view, it should be extended to a number of others.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
In my opinion, this bill on hate literature should also apply to political parties.
I remember another example too. During the last election campaign, a member of this government-and I am sorry that he is not sitting here today because I would have liked him to correct me if need be-the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Mar-chand) said in a speech at the Colisee in Quebec City these words that I quote from memory. The substance of his remarks could be summed up thus: The time is past when an English-speaking Prime Minister would come and talk to us in broken French to put forward political arguments.
In my opinion, the effect of such a statement will be to incite a collectivity or a group of individuals to hate. One individual will be hated because others do not share his ideas. Maybe that was the type of example the minister had in mind when he prepared Bill C-3. I hope my remarks will have the result of alleviating the minister's omissions when drawing up his bill.
November 17, 1969

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Organized groups often have legal and financial means to fight their cases in court. Unfortunately, the isolated individual who must appear in court must pay for the proceedings. This is a somewhat heavy burden for individuals and the law which seeks to establish a just society could protect not only integrated and organized groups but also the individual who might be the victim of injustice as in the cases I mentioned earlier.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

maintopic: GRAIN-BOX CAR DISTRIBUTION-OPPORTUNITY FOR OPPOSITION MEMBERS TO MEET RAILWAY OFFICIALS
GRAIN-BOX CAR DISTRIBUTION-OPPORTUNITY FOR OPPOSITION MEMBERS TO MEET RAILWAY OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 4 I posed a question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) with regard to the opportunity of holding a meeting with the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific managements to discuss the distribution of box cars in the prairies. The question was as follows:
I have a question for the Minister of Transport. In view of the meeting called by the Minister of Transport with Canadian Pacific and Canadian National management concerning distribution of box cars to grain shipping points in southern Saskatchewan, to which only Liberal Members of Parliament and Senators from Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba were invited, would the minister now arrange a similar meeting for opposition M.P.'s and Senators in order that we may tell railroad management the problems in our constituencies as well?
Since the question was not allowed at the time, I asked that it be put on the late-night show. In an article of October 30, 1969, the Moose Jaw Times Herald reported the following:
Canada's two major railways came under criticism here Wednesday at a private meeting called to discuss the distribution of box cars to grain shipping points in southern Saskatchewan.
The meeting was called by Transport Minister Donald Jamieson ... Besides Mr. Jamieson, Agriculture Minister H. A. Olson and the minister responsible for the Wheat Board, Otto Lang, attended, together with Liberal M.P.'s and senators from Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba.
[Mr. Valade.)
The Canadian National Railway was represented by its president, N. J. McMillan and a vice-president, Eric Stevenson and the C.P.R. by S. Gossage and M. W. Malcolm.
During the two hour discussion, which Mr. Douglas described as a frank exchange of opinions, Mr. Douglas read a five page brief which he had prepared. He outlined the general problem of box car distribution and cited a number of specific cases where there had been very few box cars available at certain shipping points in the present crop year. These cases had been brought to his attention by farmers in his own riding-
I should like to suggest that if it is the responsibility of M.P.s and the rest of Canada to be considered, why was not an open meeting held at that time? I suggest that the Minister of Transport had ample opportunity to refer the specific item to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, at which there could have been a frank discussion of the whole situation regarding the distribution of box cars. Instead of that, a meeting was held to discuss this problem-a secluded, private, invitational, furtive meeting at which only closed-mind Liberals were present. This is a further indication of the fear of this government to face problems with which we are confronted today. Further, it is contempt of the elected representatives of this nation, and it is outright discrimination by the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) against this democratic institution of the people of Canada.
It has always been my opinion that once the election is over we should unite together in this House, face problems as a group and try to do something about them. In this particular situation all we had was an invitation sent only to Liberal M.P.s from the prairies, plus some Senators, and no invitation extended to anyone else. Surely the Minister of Transport must know better than that. Surely the release issued at the end of this secluded meeting proves that the government is to blame for the disposition of box cars.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope I may be allowed the one minute of my time which was used up when the hon. member interrupted me. I was just saying that in my opinion the government has a responsibility to co-ordinate the movement of box cars.
If at any time the top management of the CPR and CNR appear before a committee of this House, or any other meeting in this House, the people we represent are entitled to a fair representation at that meeting. I quote further from the newspaper article to which I referred:
He-
Meaning the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas).
-said the railways pointed out that there were many organizations involved in the problem and that there was often not enough information passed along. They denied that the fault could be laid at the door of the train crews themselves.
This was an inquisition with respect to the train crews who were not able to defend themselves, but the railway management corrected the record when they said that the blame could not be laid at the door of the train crews. It is highly disorganized government when a situation like this is allowed to exist, when the people of Canada are not given adequate representation.
I ask the minister in all sincerity to make sure that in a similar situation in the future, fair representation is given to all of us. Further, I ask him to bring in terms of reference that will allow this House to call the management of the CPR and CNR before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, where we can have a thorough and open-minded discussion about the entire situation.

speechtext:
May I say that in many other cases I have included members of the hon. member's party and have brought together all people that I could get hold of, anyone who would be involved in the matter, to discuss it with them. For instance, I recall that in the matter of the tugboat problem in the city of Vancouver I arranged meetings for representatives of the hon. member's party, and may I say there have been many other cases where at the request of members I have gone into their constituencies. In fact, I see one hon. member present, a member of the Progressive Conservative Party, with whom I met a very large delegation.
All I am saying is that in this particular case I followed what has been my custom ever since I have had these responsibilities, and that has been to do the best I could to answer the request of a specific member. I want to commend the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas) for having had the initiative to ask if such a meeting could be arranged in this case. It was arranged at his instigation.
So far as members of parties opposite are concerned, if the hon. member would like the same kind of consideration, and if indeed he had asked me for it I think the record reveals he would have obtained it. There was nothing in this particular incident that was any different from the half dozen or more I have already mentioned, and in fact from many more which do not come readily to my mind at the moment.
The simple truth of the matter is that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas) asked for this; I was able to arrange it for him and was glad to do so. I remind the hon. member that if he wants the same kind of discussion on this or any other subject, I shall do my best to do as much for him. Of course, I cannot command. Perhaps I might be able to use more persuasion with the CNR than with the CPR, but certainly I will be happy to help the hon. member.
If my hon. friend feels that is not an honest representation of the facts, I can only ask him to go back to the record and talk to the members of his party. If at any time a request has been made to me, to any official of any government agency or to any private organization, which directly relates to transportation and I have turned him down or tried in any way to evade that request, I will be glad to apologize to him or any other member in this House.
November 17, 1969

maintopic: POST OFFICE-REQUEST FOR REDUCTION OF RATES ON NON-PROFIT PUBLICATIONS
POST OFFICE-REQUEST FOR REDUCTION OF RATES ON NON-PROFIT PUBLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that I have to keep my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) up late, as I did on more than one occasion in the previous session. The questions discussed and matters raised were of importance, and for me it was an education to be called the many names that I was called in the previous session by the minister. I was designated as a Cassandra, as Falstaff and as the Merry Monk of Hillsborough. As I heard this and my education broadened, I declared that even members of the opposition should have at their disposal large cadres of speech writers and public relations men that they, too, could find such charming names for other people. I am wrong, perhaps, in not indulging in name calling but I feel that by pointing to the administration of the minister's department I have said enough. I know the minister grows impatient and wishes to express his displeasure at hearing the same problems aired time and again. May I say that the only solution is for him to cure the ills of which we speak.
One of the consistent themes which I and others in this House have stressed has been the danger to the free flow of ideas resulting from severe restrictions on many publications in this country. Indeed, the minister was consistent, too-I give him credit for that- because he shrugged off our warnings and declared that for a few cents more this or that publication could meet the new impositions. But while he was going about reassuring the House and country, important organs of thought and opinion were dying, as we said would be the case and as the publishers told him would be the case. But the minister knew better; he knew more than the publishers, more than the people and more than the opposition. And what happened?
May I read a few excerpts from the press which tell the unhappy tale. The Gazette of

July 9, 1969, carries this headline over an article: "Mail purge killed 2,500 publications". An earlier report indicates that Montreal, that most interesting magazine, has gone out of business because of cost. Another headline of October 21, 1969, reads: "Death of 30 publications blamed on mail rate rise". In the body of the article is found the following:
A Cross-Canada Survey by The Canadian Press shows at least 30 publications of this type ceased publication this year, their deaths attributed to the higher rates.
Another headline carried in the Toronto Telegram of October 2, 1969, reads: "Postal rate jump lethal for some trade magazines". So the story goes; so we see the diminution in the number of these very important organs of thought and opinion, and so the unhappy tale grows more and more unhappy.
Only last week, Mr. Speaker, a concerned and well informed group of Canadians, the Committee for Fair Postal Rates, came to Ottawa. They argued cogently and well. They were well received by many members, but when they presented their case to the Postmaster General they received not encouragement but rejection. The minister became the rejector general of publications, so to speak. In addition to that they were given a little lecture on, of all things, the perils of exaggeration. The minister said, as reported by Donald Newman of the Globe and Mail:
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
"You would do your case much more justice if you didn't exaggerate ... this kind of exaggeration makes us doubt anything you say."
This warning against exaggeration, believe it or not, was delivered on the day following the Postmaster General's Toronto dissertation where he raised those unhelpful and unwarranted problems about the work of the provinces in the field of constitutional reform. That speech will not go down in history as an example of measured appraisal or balanced judgment. The warning came from the man who in the last session used to tell us how well things were working out in his new department, how the new sorting procedures were so happily received by the workers, how well everything was going in terms of administration. We were told at length of all the improved techniques and management, but there was a pause in these rosy declamations after the blistering report of chief adjudicator Martin.
In fact, all is not well in the non-profit publications field. There is great danger that
November 17, 1969

this continuing rigidity of attitude will diminish still further the flow of informed thought and opinion so essential to a true and enlightened democracy. While orders of government still are disseminated freely and easily-and on occasion I understand some organs of the national Liberal party have the same blessing

opinions of private groups are diminished in their effectiveness as they seek to stimulate public opinion and to provide background information.
I think instead of lecturing, the minister would have been well advised to listen. Despite the glamour of other esoteric means of communication-and we hear a lot about those fascinating and delightful objects of exultation-there is still a place for the written word in our society. Old-fashioned mail is still important and Canadians still like to receive it.
A man in Toronto heard so much about the mail delays that he sent a letter to himself with a six cent stamp on it. He got it back in Toronto in ten days. He now has some means of measuring the delays. Opinion magazines and publications-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I object to the hyperbole, rhetoric and coarse exaggeration within which the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) shrouds his questions. I wish to give two examples of the kind of statements the hon. member makes. At page 687 of Hansard the hon. member made the statement that when he returned to Parliament this fall he found that about one-quarter of the floor space in the foyer, that is the wash room, had been pre-empted. When he asked about this he was told that it was to be the new domain of the Minister of Communications, so he said the expansion was indeed physical as well as intellectual and jurisdictional. I was in the House at the time. These words would have remained in Hansard had I not risen to my feet and said, "Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, the information is false." I was not only shocked by that statement but deeply shocked by his reply. The reply was:
I have been corrected, Mr. Speaker, and I stand corrected. As I stand crowded in the future I will remember that it is not this minister . . . who is responsible.

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
At page 769 of Hansard the hon. member made another statement which is equally false. It reads in part:
-not a free rate, like the National Liberal Federation, but a much better rate than they are now paying?
The hon. member said the Montreal magazine had gone out of existence because of the increase in postal rates. But as I have said before, the decision affecting that magazine had been taken months ear her. He quoted two headlines, one saying that 2,500 publications had gone out of existence and another, over a CP article of a later date, stating that 30 publications had gone out of existence. Which is true? One of them is exaggerated. Are these equivocal statements meant to be misleading and inaccurate? Is this a deliberate attempt to deceive?
The hon. member relies on the group which came to see me. They, too, exaggerated, but they could only bring forward the cases of four periodicals which they said had ceased publication, including La Tere de Chez Nous. But it has not ceased publication, Mr. Speaker, and the mere statement that it had done so caused La Terre de Chez Nous to take advertizing space at great expense to say: All is going well with us, thank you.
The hon. member mentioned a British Columbia trade union publication. All that was necessary in that case was to increase the subscription rate from $1.00 a year to $1.43. Mr. Speaker, we were carrying 770,000 issues of that publication in a year for $1,000. I ask you, is there anyone in this House who would undertake similar work on those terms?
In conclusion, may I say this: It is easy for certain publishers and hon. members to bring pressure against increases in postage rates and lead the public to believe that the Post Office is crushing Canadian publications. It is most difficult to get over to them the fact that it costs money to carry newspapers and periodicals in the mails, and that if they do not pay for it the taxpayers generally must do so.

maintopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-POSSIBLE NICKEL AND COPPER PRICE INCREASES-ACTION BY GOVERNMENT
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-POSSIBLE NICKEL AND COPPER PRICE INCREASES-ACTION BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Friday last while the union membership was voting in favour of a new contract providing for a substantial wage increase, I
November 17, 1969

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) what action the government was contemplating to prevent a subsequent increase in the cost of nickel and copper. The Prime Minister told me that he would make sure that the question would be brought to the attention of the minister concerned.
I am pleased to have the opportunity to discuss this matter in the house this evening and to set forth during the few minutes at my disposal the baneful consequences that such a price increase would have on the cost of living not only in the Sudbury area but also throughout the country.
Mr. Speaker, the precedent is well established throughout the country. Indeed, when a company grants a salary increase to its employees, an increase in the prices for consumer products follows almost automatically. I suggest that this vicious circle must be broken at all costs if there is to be an end to inflation.
The problem is getting more and more serious in the Sudbury area. Lately, many groups of organized workers have obtained fairly large increases in salary and I am happy about it for their sake. However, such increases become meaningless as a consequential increase in prices immediately follows. And to make the situation more abnormal still, a large number of unorganized workers do not get equal increases in salary but have to pay the same prices as the others for products and services, and as a result the number poor people increases considerably.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, following this new contract at the International Nickel Company, in Sudbury, one may expect an imminent increase in nickel and copper prices. Moreover, it is well known that such an increase will automatically bring about a similar increase in consumer prices in the Sudbury area. One fears, and not without cause, that companies, distributors, tradesmen, realtors, contractors, professionals, will take advantage of that rise in the workers' income to increase their prices sharply.
That is a most alarming situation if one takes into account that the cost of living in the Sudbury area is already higher than in the most areas of Ontario. Therefore I insist firstly that the Prices and Incomes Commission investigate the matter and determine immediately whether at present an increase in the price of nickel is warranted, so that the increase does not threaten the economic stability of the country; and secondly, that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs bring every necessary pressure to bear on companies, distributors, dealers, etc., so that they do not take advantage of the situation by increasing their prices.
Mr. Speaker, it is my opinion that government leaders will have to take a firmer stand and exercise more control if they are to break up the vicious circle of the wage-price spiral and thus bring to an end this frenzied rush towards inflation.
According to recent statements by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) had the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford), we have every reason to believe that the government is more willing than ever before to take whatever steps are necessary and I dare hope that my representations will be followed up.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul Langlois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
maintopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-POSSIBLE NICKEL AND COPPER PRICE INCREASES-ACTION BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am well aware of the interest the hon. member for Nickel Belt takes in the consumers of Canada, and particularly in those of his constituency.
He gives a clear and detailed account of a situation, and he also proves all the consideration he has for his fellow citizens.

We all, of course, deplore unnecessary price increases, and I am sure that the House is well aware of the need for restraint at this time. The comments of the hon. member will be drawn to the attention of the minister and they will receive every attention.
